Advocacy
Undue influence
Adverse interest

questions.explanation: An undue influence threat exists when client management uses pressure, such as threatening to replace the firm, to coerce the auditor into a judgment. Escalating within the firm instead of yielding is a safeguard against it. Self-interest is about the auditor's own financial stake (for example, a loan from the client). Advocacy is promoting the client's position. Adverse interest arises when the client and the firm are in, or threaten, litigation against each other.

questions.prompt:
After a smooth audit, an attest client sends the engagement manager an expensive designer watch as thanks. The CPA firm has no written policy on client gifts.

What should the manager do, consistent with the AICPA Code on gifts and entertainment?

options.text: Accept the gift, because the firm's policy does not expressly prohibit it.
Ask the client to present the watch to the CPA firm as a whole instead of to the manager personally.
Accept the gift, but only after the audit report has been released.
Evaluate whether a reasonable observer would see the gift as compromising objectivity.

questions.explanation: Under the Code's conceptual framework, the question is whether a reasonable and informed third party would conclude that objectivity or independence is impaired. For an attest client, accepting a gift impairs independence unless its value is clearly insignificant to the recipient; an expensive watch is not. A silent firm policy is not permission, redirecting the gift to the firm doesn't remove the threat, and timing after the report doesn't help because the relationship continues.

questions.prompt:
An attest client invites the audit manager to an annual customer-appreciation dinner and baseball game that the client also hosts for its key vendors and customers. The manager would attend with client executives.

How does the AICPA Code treat this entertainment?

options.text: It is acceptable if it is reasonable in the circumstances (nature, frequency, value, purpose).
It always impairs independence, because any entertainment received from an attest client is prohibited by the Code.
It is acceptable without any evaluation, because other vendors were invited too.
It is acceptable only if the manager reimburses the client for the full cost.

questions.explanation: The Code treats gifts and entertainment differently. Gifts from an attest client must be clearly insignificant. Entertainment is allowed when it is reasonable in the circumstances, judged by factors such as its nature, the occasion, cost and frequency, whether it has a business purpose, and whether client personnel attend. A blanket ban overstates the rule, an invitation list doesn't remove the need to evaluate, and reimbursement is not required.

questions.prompt:
Hollis & Co. CPAs keeps the books and prepares the tax returns for Ridgeview Bakery, a small private company. A competing firm claims Hollis has violated the AICPA Independence Rule by providing both services.

Has Hollis violated the Independence Rule?

options.text: Yes, because providing two services to one client creates a familiarity threat.
No, because the client is the main beneficiary and keeps management responsibility
No, because the firm assigns different CPAs to the bookkeeping work and to the tax work.
Yes, because combining the services jeopardizes the public interest.

questions.explanation:
WGU keys this as no violation, reasoning that the client is the main beneficiary of the services. Under the AICPA Code, bookkeeping and tax preparation are permitted nonattest services. If Ridgeview is also an attest client, they are allowed when the client assumes all management responsibilities, designates a competent person to oversee the services, evaluates the results, and accepts responsibility for them. Using different staff doesn't create or cure independence, and there is no automatic familiarity or public-interest violation.

Textbook vs. current law: the Code's real test is the general requirements for nonattest services (ET 1.295.040), including that the CPA not assume management responsibilities (ET 1.295.030), not who benefits. For an SEC issuer audit client, SOX bans bookkeeping outright (see the next question).
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-2: "AICPA Code: Independence Considerations for Members in Public Practice" section

questions.prompt:
Arden Manufacturing, an SEC registrant, asks its external audit firm to take over its bookkeeping and to prepare its federal income tax return.

What is the correct analysis under SOX and the SEC/PCAOB independence rules?

options.text: The firm may do both, as long as different partners lead the bookkeeping engagement and the tax engagement.
No bookkeeping for an issuer audit client; tax work only with audit committee preapproval.
The firm may do both, as long as the fees are disclosed in the proxy statement.
The firm may do neither, because SOX bans all tax services for audit clients.

questions.explanation: Section 201 of SOX lists nonaudit services an auditor may not provide to an issuer audit client, including bookkeeping, financial information systems design, appraisal, actuarial, internal audit outsourcing, management functions, broker-dealer, and legal services. Tax services are not banned, but they must be preapproved by the audit committee (also PCAOB Rule 3524). Staffing and fee disclosure don't cure a prohibited service, and SOX doesn't ban tax services outright.

questions.prompt: Which fee arrangement is prohibited under the AICPA Code's contingent fee rule?

questions.prompt:
At the planning meeting, the audit partner tells the team: "Don't take management's word for anything. Keep a questioning mind and critically assess every piece of evidence you collect."

Integrity

Due care

Integrity is honesty and not subordinating judgment; objectivity and independence are freedom from conflicts and bias. The public interest is the broader duty to the people who rely on the work.

What is the auditor's most appropriate defense?

options.text: Argue lack of privity, since the client never contracted with the auditor
Use contributory negligence to be completely absolved of any liability
Assert comparative negligence to apportion the damages
Invoke the audit-interference rule to put all of the fault on the client

questions.explanation: Courts now let accountants assert comparative negligence, which replaced the harsh all-or-nothing contributory negligence approach with an allocation of fault, and juries apportion damages between the accountant and the client. The client is in privity with the auditor, so lack of privity fails. Contributory negligence as a complete bar is the outdated approach. The audit-interference rule limits the client-negligence defense to cases where the client actually interfered with the audit; it doesn't let the auditor shift all fault to the client.

questions.prompt:
Investors sue an auditor under Section 11 of the Securities Act of 1933 over misstatements in audited financial statements included in a registration statement.

What must the auditor show to win with a due diligence defense?

options.text: The plaintiffs did not read or rely on the registration statement when they bought the securities.
The misstatement was not material to an average prudent investor.
The statute of limitations had already expired before the investors filed the suit.
It made a reasonable investigation and had reasonable grounds to believe the statements were true.

questions.explanation: The due diligence defense for an expert such as an auditor under Section 11(b)(3) requires showing a reasonable investigation and reasonable grounds for believing the expertised statements were true. In other words, the auditor wasn't negligent or fraudulent. Lack of reliance, immateriality, and the statute of limitations are separate defenses, not due diligence. Section 11 plaintiffs generally don't have to prove reliance at all.

questions.prompt:
A U.S. company's regional director pays a local agent a large "consulting fee" to win approval of a foreign operating license. When charged under the FCPA, the director argues he did not know the agent would pass money to a government official.

Which amendment to the FCPA set the "knowing" standard this defense relies on?

options.text: The Trade Act of 1974
The Federal Trade Commission Act
The International Anti-Bribery and Fair Competition Act of 1998
The Omnibus Trade and Competitiveness Act of 1988

questions.explanation:
WGU keys the Omnibus Trade and Competitiveness Act of 1988. It amended the FCPA to replace the looser "reason to know" standard for payments through third parties with a "knowing" standard, added the affirmative defenses (local law; reasonable and bona fide expenditures), and clarified the facilitating-payment exception. The 1998 act extended the FCPA to foreign companies and persons; the other acts aren't FCPA amendments.

Textbook vs. current law: "knowing" includes awareness of a high probability that the payment would reach an official (willful blindness). A director who deliberately avoids learning the facts can still be liable.

questions.prompt:
A U.S. equipment maker pays airfare and modest hotel costs for foreign health-ministry officials to visit its U.S. plant and see a demonstration of the devices the ministry is considering buying.

options.text: The local law defense
The facilitating payment exception
The bona fide expenditure defense
The materiality defense

The local law defense requires that the payment be lawful under the foreign country's written laws. The facilitating-payment exception covers small payments to speed up routine governmental actions, not travel to market products. Materiality isn't an FCPA defense.

questions.prompt:
An investor sues an audit firm under Rule 10b-5, claiming millions in losses after the client's stock collapsed. The firm shows the stock fell along with the whole sector during a market-wide crash.

Which defense does the precedent in Maxwell v. KPMG LLP support?

options.text: The investor's loss was a direct result of the misleading statements in the audit opinion.
The investor's harm was caused by the market in general, not by the auditor's statements.
The firm acted intentionally, so the PSLRA limits its damages.
The firm cannot be sued under Rule 10b-5, because it is not the issuer.

questions.explanation:
A Rule 10b-5 plaintiff must prove, among other elements, that the damages resulted from the misstatement: loss causation. In Maxwell v. KPMG, the court found the harm wasn't caused by KPMG's audit; the company's collapse came from broader market forces. So a firm can defend by showing the loss came from the market, not its statements. The first choice is the plaintiff's argument. Intentional conduct removes protection rather than adding it, and auditors can be sued under 10b-5.

Case note: Maxwell v. KPMG LLP, 520 F.3d 713 (7th Cir. 2008) was actually a state-law negligence suit by marchFIRST's bankruptcy trustee, not a 10b-5 case. Judge Posner borrowed the securities-law idea of loss causation and held that the dot-com bust, not KPMG's audit, caused the collapse. Your text places it under Rule 10b-5, so answer it that way on the exam.

questions.prompt: According to your Mintz text, which law increased auditors' liability by specifying or expanding the scope of third parties to whom an auditor owes a duty of care?

options.text: The Dodd-Frank Act
The Private Securities Litigation Reform Act
The Securities Exchange Act of 1934
The Sarbanes-Oxley Act

questions.explanation:
Mintz states that SOX increases auditor liability to third parties by specifying or expanding the scope of third parties to whom an auditor owes a duty of care, including through the Section 404 internal control reporting requirements. Dodd-Frank deals with whistleblowers and financial reform, the PSLRA limits auditor liability (proportionate liability, pleading standards), and the 1934 Act regulates trading and ongoing reporting.

Textbook vs. current law: who can sue an auditor for negligence is still set mainly by state common law (Ultramares, Credit Alliance, the Restatement, Rosenblum). SOX adds federal duties and reporting, not a new common-law duty. Answer SOX on the exam.

questions.prompt:
A large corporation and its much smaller audit firm are both sued for securities fraud. The jury finds the audit firm 10% responsible and finds it did not knowingly commit the violation.

How does the PSLRA affect the audit firm?

options.text: It pays damages only in proportion to its share of responsibility.
It cannot settle out of court unless the corporation settles too.
It is liable by default, because intent does not have to be established.
It is held to the same standard as the corporation under joint and several liability.

questions.explanation: The PSLRA dropped joint-and-several liability for non-knowing securities violations and adopted proportionate liability: a defendant pays only the share of damages it is responsible for. Only those who knowingly commit securities fraud remain jointly and severally liable. The PSLRA doesn't tie one defendant's settlement to another's, and it raised rather than removed the need to plead scienter.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-4: "Private Securities Litigation Reform Act (PSLRA)" section

questions.prompt:
Investors sue a biotech company and its auditor, alleging they overstated a drug trial's success to lift the share price.

Under the PSLRA, what must the investors do to plead the auditor's fraud liability?

options.text: Show only that the investors suffered economic harm from the misinformation
Show facts that a reasonable person would see as intentional conduct by the auditor
Nothing, because the burden of proof shifts to the auditor under the PSLRA
Show that the investors completed their own due diligence on the drug before buying the shares

questions.explanation:
WGU phrases this as showing that a reasonable person would see the firm's actions as intentional. The PSLRA requires plaintiffs to plead with particularity facts giving rise to a strong inference of scienter, through strong circumstantial evidence of conscious misbehavior or recklessness, or through motive and opportunity. Economic loss alone isn't enough, the burden doesn't shift to the auditor, and the investors' own due diligence isn't an element.

Case note: in Tellabs v. Makor (2007), the Supreme Court held a complaint survives "only if a reasonable person would deem the inference of scienter cogent and at least as compelling as any opposing inference one could draw from the facts alleged." That's the source of WGU's 'reasonable person' wording.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-4: "Private Securities Litigation Reform Act (PSLRA)" section

questions.prompt:
A lender that was never a party to the audit engagement lends money to a company based on its audited statements and later sues the auditor for ordinary negligence. The jurisdiction follows Ultramares v. Touche.

What is the auditor's best defense?

options.text: Lack of privity, since the lender had no contract with the auditor
Contributory negligence: the lender should have done its own analysis
Due diligence: the auditor made a reasonable investigation under Section 11
Proportionate liability: the PSLRA caps the auditor's share of damages

questions.explanation: Under Ultramares v. Touche (1931), a third party not in contractual privity with the auditor cannot sue for ordinary negligence, although the court left open claims for gross negligence and fraud. (Your slide 8 shows 1933, but the case was decided January 6, 1931.) Due diligence is a Securities Act Section 11 defense, and proportionate liability is a federal securities rule. Nothing in the facts shows the lender was careless, and lack of privity defeats the claim outright without any need to prove the lender's fault.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-1: "Legal Liabilities of Auditors: An Overview" section

questions.prompt:
A bank sues an auditor for negligence. The auditor knew the company would give its audited statements to this bank for a specific loan, but the auditor never sent the report to the bank, never talked to the bank, and did nothing to encourage the bank's reliance.

Under the near-privity test as sharpened in Security Pacific v. Peat Marwick, what is the auditor's best defense?

options.text: The auditor never conveyed the report to the bank or induced its reliance
The bank was not a reasonably foreseeable user of the financial statements
The audit was performed in accordance with GAAS, so no negligence is possible
The bank's loss was caused by a market downturn rather than by anything in the audited statements

questions.explanation: Credit Alliance v. Arthur Andersen set three near-privity tests: the auditor knew the statements would be used for a particular purpose, by a known party who intended to rely, and there was conduct linking the auditor to that party. Security Pacific sharpened the third test: the auditor must directly convey the report to the third party or act to induce its reliance. Without that link, the near-privity claim fails. Foreseeability is a broader standard that near-privity states don't use. GAAS compliance is evidence of due care but not an automatic bar. Market causation isn't raised by these facts.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-1: "Legal Liabilities of Auditors: An Overview" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 16 (Near-Privity Relationship: Credit Alliance; Security Pacific)
Credit Alliance Corp. v. Arthur Andersen & Co., 65 N.Y.2d 536 (1985)
Security Pacific Business Credit, Inc. v. Peat Marwick Main & Co., 79 N.Y.2d 695 (1992)
Your Objective Assessment notes, Ch. 8 (near-privity: directly convey report; induce reliance)
New for the OA Focus Review (Auditor's Defense: Suggested Study Review on OA 2)
questions.hint: Near privity needs a link between the auditor and the third party.

questions.prompt:
Several investors who never dealt with the auditor sue for negligence in a state that follows Bily v. Arthur Young.

Why does Bily give the auditor a stronger defense than a Rosenblum jurisdiction would?

options.text: Bily held that auditors are liable to all reasonably foreseeable third parties who rely on the statements.
Bily held that auditors can never be sued by anyone except the SEC for negligent audits.
Bily allowed 'grapevine' plaintiffs who heard about the statements from others to sue.
Bily rejected the foreseeability approach for negligence claims by investors.

questions.explanation: The California Supreme Court in Bily v. Arthur Young (1992) rejected the Rosenblum foreseeability rule, reasoning that it exposes auditors to liability far beyond their proportionate share. It limited general negligence liability to the client, and it allowed only specifically intended, known beneficiaries of the report to sue for negligent misrepresentation. Rosenblum (New Jersey, 1983) is the case that extended liability to all reasonably foreseeable third parties. The grapevine-plaintiff ruling came later in Murphy v. BDO Seidman, and auditors can be sued by private parties, not just the SEC.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-1: "Legal Liabilities of Auditors: An Overview" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slides 19–20 (Reasonably Foreseeable Third Parties: Rosenblum; Bily; Murphy v. BDO Seidman)
Bily v. Arthur Young & Co., 3 Cal. 4th 370 (1992)
H. Rosenblum, Inc. v. Adler, 93 N.J. 324 (1983)

questions.prompt:
A client sues its auditor for negligence after a large receivable proved uncollectible. The auditor raises the due care defense based on the prudent person concept.

Which showing is part of that defense?

options.text: The client did not suffer any real economic loss from writing off the uncollectible receivable.
The auditor acted without any intent to deceive the client, so the auditor cannot be negligent.
It had the needed skills and used them with reasonable care, diligence, and good faith.
The statute of limitations expired before the client filed the claim.

questions.explanation: The due care defense rests on the prudent person concept: the auditor possessed the requisite skills, employed them with reasonable care and diligence, and acted in good faith and with integrity. An auditor isn't liable for errors in judgment. No loss and the statute of limitations are separate defenses. Lack of intent is a defense to fraud, not to negligence, which needs no intent.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-2: "Auditor Defenses to Negligence and Fraud" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 31 (Auditor Defenses for Negligence: due care defense)
Your Objective Assessment notes, Ch. 8 (Due Care Defense: prudent person concept)
New for the OA Focus Review (Auditor's Defense: Suggested Study Review on OA 2)
questions.hint: Prudent person: skills, care, good faith.

questions.prompt:
An investor who read a company's audited statements in a newspaper article sues the auditor for negligent misrepresentation in a jurisdiction that follows McCamish.

What is the auditor's strongest defense?

options.text: The investor wasn't a known person relying for a known purpose.
The auditor didn't intend to deceive the investor or anyone else who read the article.
The client was partly negligent in preparing the statements.
The misstatement was discovered before the investor sold any shares.

questions.explanation: McCamish (a 1999 Texas Supreme Court case about a law firm, which Mintz applies to auditors) sets a strict standard for negligent misrepresentation: the plaintiff must be a known person who relies on the auditor's representations for a known purpose. An anonymous newspaper reader isn't. Intent to deceive is irrelevant to negligent misrepresentation, which doesn't require intent. Client negligence is a defense in malpractice suits by the client. The timing of discovery doesn't defeat the claim.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-2: "Auditor Defenses to Negligence and Fraud" section

McCamish, Martin, Brown & Loeffler v. F.E. Appling Interests, 991 S.W.2d 787 (Tex. 1999)
Your Objective Assessment notes, Ch. 8 (negligent misrepresentation defense: known person, known purpose)
New for the OA Focus Review (Auditor's Defense: Suggested Study Review on OA 2)

questions.prompt:
A client sues its auditor for malpractice. The auditor shows that the client's controller hid bank statements and lied to the audit team about unrecorded liabilities, which kept the auditor from finding the problem.

How does this affect the auditor's defense?

options.text: It doesn't matter, because client conduct is never a defense to audit malpractice.
The client's negligence is a defense because it caused the auditor's failure.
It shifts the case to Section 11 of the Securities Act, where due diligence is the only defense.
It proves the auditor committed fraud, because the auditor relied on false representations.

questions.explanation: Contributory negligence of the client can be a defense to malpractice, but only when the client's negligence proximately contributed to the accountant's failure to perform the contract and report the truth, as when the client actively hides records or lies to the auditors. Under comparative negligence, the client's share of fault reduces the auditor's damages. Client conduct is a recognized defense, Section 11 applies only to registration statements, and relying on a client's lies is not fraud by the auditor.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-2: "Auditor Defenses to Negligence and Fraud" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slides 11–12 (Defending Audit-Malpractice Cases; Comparative Negligence)
New for the OA Focus Review (Auditor's Defense: Suggested Study Review on OA 2)

questions.prompt:
Investors sue an auditor for fraud under common law.

Which showing would defeat the claim?

options.text: The auditor didn't perform a test of controls over the area that was misstated.
The auditor's fee for the engagement was lower than the fees of other firms.
The auditor didn't send the report directly to the investors or speak with them about it.
The auditor didn't know it was untrue and had no intent to deceive.

questions.explanation: Fraud requires scienter, so showing the auditor didn't know the representation was false and had no intent to deceive defeats it. Other fraud defenses include that the representation wasn't false or wasn't material, that the third party didn't rely on it, and that the third party suffered no damages. A missed control test points to possible negligence; it is not a defense to fraud. Fee levels are irrelevant. Direct delivery matters for near-privity negligence, not fraud, which is available to any third party who relied.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-2: "Auditor Defenses to Negligence and Fraud" section

Your Objective Assessment notes, Ch. 8 (auditor defenses for fraud: did not know representation was untrue; no intent to deceive)
New for the OA Focus Review (Auditor's Defense: Suggested Study Review on OA 2)

questions.prompt:
Investors sue an audit firm for fraud. The firm shows that the investors' losses came from a lawsuit against the company that was filed after the audit report date and had nothing to do with the audited numbers.

Which defense is the firm using?

options.text: The auditor had no duty to the third party.
Any loss to the investors was caused by other events.
The third party was itself negligent.
The claim is barred by the statute of limitations.

questions.explanation: Among the defenses an auditor can raise against fraud claims is that any loss to the third party was caused by other events. Here the later lawsuit, not the audited statements, caused the loss. The other choices are also listed defenses (no duty, plaintiff's own negligence, statute of limitations), but none fits these facts.

questions.prompt:
Shareholders sue an auditor under Section 11 of the Securities Act of 1933, claiming its unqualified opinion in a registration statement was misleading because it later proved wrong. They allege only that a reasonable audit would have caught the problem.

Under the Omnicare standard as applied to auditors, what is the auditor's best defense?

options.text: Section 11 never applies to auditors, only to the company issuing the securities.
The plaintiffs must prove that the auditor intended to deceive them when it signed the opinion.
An opinion isn't false just because it proved wrong; they must name specific audit steps.
The auditor is protected because it was hired and paid by the company, not by the investors.

questions.explanation: Under Omnicare (2015), an issuer case that courts and your text apply to auditors, an opinion isn't false under Section 11 merely because it turns out to be incorrect. An auditor can be liable only if it didn't actually hold the opinion, if the opinion contains an embedded untrue statement of fact, or if it omits facts that make it misleading. For an omission claim, the plaintiff must identify actual and material steps the auditor took or didn't take, not just claim that any reasonable audit would have found the problem. Auditors are covered by Section 11, which doesn't require proof of intent, and who paid the fee is irrelevant.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-3: "Statutory Liability" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slides 40–43 (Section 11; Omnicare Opinion; Section 11 Liability Standard for Auditors; Material Omission)
Omnicare, Inc. v. Laborers District Council Construction Industry Pension Fund, 575 U.S. 175 (2015)
Your Objective Assessment notes, Ch. 8 (material omission: identify actual and material steps)
New for the OA Focus Review (Auditor's Defense: Suggested Study Review on OA 2)
questions.hint: Wrong isn't the same as false.

questions.prompt:
An investor sues an auditor under Section 18 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 over a misleading statement in a 10-K filed with the SEC. The auditor shows it followed GAAS carefully and didn't know the statement was misleading.

What is the auditor's defense, and when is it weakened?

options.text: Due diligence, but it applies only to initial public offerings
Good faith without knowledge, limited if grossly negligent
Lack of privity, but it fails whenever the investor relied on the 10-K
Proportionate liability, but only for auditors that knowingly violated the law

questions.explanation: Section 18 imposes liability for material false or misleading statements in SEC filings, but the auditor's liability can be limited if it acted in good faith and had no knowledge that the statement was false or misleading. Courts have limited the good-faith defense when the auditor's conduct was grossly negligent. Due diligence is the Securities Act Section 11 defense, privity is a common-law concept, and proportionate liability under the PSLRA protects non-knowing defendants, not knowing ones.

questions.prompt:
At a large CPA firm, partners quietly give staff the answers to a required internal continuing-education ethics exam so everyone passes on time. Other partners know and say nothing.

Under the AICPA Code, how is this conduct best classified?

options.text: A breach of the Contingent Fees Rule
A self-review threat to the firm's independence
An act discreditable to the profession
Acceptable, because the exam is internal and not a CPA licensing exam

questions.explanation:
Your slides describe exactly this: Big Four firms were caught giving staff answers to internal exams used to meet CPE requirements, and in one case the exam was on ethics. Those violations were treated as an act discreditable to the profession. The behavior has nothing to do with fees or with auditing one's own work, and an internal exam still certifies required professional education.

The bank was more negligent than the auditor, so comparative fault bars any recovery by the bank.
The audit was performed in accordance with GAAS, so a negligence claim is legally impossible against the firm.
The statute of limitations always bars bank claims.

questions.explanation: Credit Alliance requires (1) the auditor's knowledge that the statements will be used for a particular purpose, (2) a known party intending to rely, and (3) some conduct linking the auditor to that party. Security Pacific sharpened the third element: the auditor must directly convey the report or act to induce reliance. None of these exists. Comparative fault and limitations aren't supported by the facts, and following GAAS is evidence of due care but doesn't make negligence impossible.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-1: "Legal Liabilities of Auditors: An Overview" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 16 (Common Law Liability to Third Parties: Near-Privity Relationship)
Credit Alliance Corp. v. Arthur Andersen & Co., 65 N.Y.2d 536 (1985)
Security Pacific Business Credit, Inc. v. Peat Marwick Main & Co., 79 N.Y.2d 695 (1992)
questions.hint: What three things does Credit Alliance require?

questions.prompt:
A client sues its auditor after a loan-loss estimate the auditor accepted proves too low. The auditor shows the team had the right expertise, gathered and evaluated evidence carefully, acted honestly, and that the estimate was reasonable when made.

Which defense is the auditor using?

options.text: The due care defense: an auditor isn't liable for good-faith errors in judgment.
The comparative negligence defense, because the client chose to keep the estimate
The lack of reliance defense, because the client never read the auditor's workpapers
The Section 11 materiality defense

questions.explanation: The due care defense rests on the prudent-person concept: the auditor had the needed skills, used them with reasonable care and diligence, acted in good faith and with integrity, and is not liable for errors in judgment. Comparative negligence allocates fault to the client, lack of reliance is a fraud defense, and materiality is a Section 11 defense.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-2: "Auditor Defenses to Negligence and Fraud" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 31 (Auditor Defenses for Negligence (prudent person; not liable for errors in judgment))
questions.hint: Skill, care, good faith, and an honest judgment call.

questions.prompt:
An audit senior notices that the client's largest customer confirmation came back with a different balance. To finish on time, she decides not to follow up and signs off, knowing the difference could be significant. It later turns out to be a material misstatement.

Which basic theory of liability fits her conduct?

options.text: Ordinary negligence
Fraud with intent to deceive
Breach of contract only
Recklessness

questions.explanation: Recklessness is conduct short of intent to cause harm but greater than simple negligence. Negligence is unknowingly taking a risk one should have been aware of. Recklessness is knowingly taking a risk, which is what she did by skipping follow-up she knew was needed. Nothing shows she intended to deceive anyone, and the facts go beyond a contract dispute.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-2: "Auditor Defenses to Negligence and Fraud" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 13 (Recklessness)
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 21 (Gross Negligence and Fraud)
Your PA Attempt 2 (passed), Q21: same concept, WGU-keyed answer
questions.hint: Did she know about the risk and take it anyway?

questions.prompt:
For three years, an audit firm knew that a long-time client's managers were stealing inventory and chose not to report it. The firm knew investors relying on the statements would lose millions.

Which basic theory of liability establishes the firm's liability?

options.text: Negligence
Opportunity
Willfulness
Rationalization

questions.explanation: WGU keys knowing, deliberate failure to report, with awareness of the harm, as willfulness. Negligence is carelessness without knowledge. Opportunity and rationalization are fraud-triangle elements that explain why people commit fraud; they aren't theories of the auditor's legal liability.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-2: "Auditor Defenses to Negligence and Fraud" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 13 (Recklessness (knowing vs. unknowing risk))
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 21 (Gross Negligence and Fraud (scienter))
Your PA Attempt 2 (passed), Q22: same concept, WGU-keyed answer
questions.hint: The firm knew and chose not to act.

questions.prompt:
A supplier extended credit to a company after reading its audited statements. When the company failed, the supplier sued the auditor for common-law fraud. The supplier can show the statements were false and that it relied on them and lost money.

What else must the supplier specifically prove?

options.text: The auditor failed to follow every requirement of generally accepted auditing standards
The auditor knew the statements were false and intended to deceive (scienter).
The auditor owed the supplier a contractual duty of care arising from the audit engagement letter
The auditor charged a contingent fee

questions.explanation: Common-law fraud requires a false representation, the accountant's knowledge or belief that it was false, intent to induce reliance (scienter), reliance by the third party, and damages. The missing element here is scienter. A GAAS departure points to negligence, a contractual duty is about privity (fraud claims are open to any third party), and the fee arrangement is irrelevant.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-1: "Legal Liabilities of Auditors: An Overview" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 17 (Plaintiff Claims Under Common Law)
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 24 (Common Law Liability for Fraud)
Your PA Attempt 2 (passed), Q20: same concept, WGU-keyed answer
questions.hint: What separates fraud from negligence?

questions.prompt:
An auditor knew its client would give the audited statements to "our trade creditors" when asking for credit terms, though the auditor never learned which creditors. One of those creditors sues for negligent misrepresentation under the Restatement (Second) of Torts approach.

Why does the auditor's defense that it never knew this particular creditor fail?

options.text: Negligent misrepresentation claims require only that the creditor be foreseeable to anyone.
The creditor heard about the statements secondhand, which always creates liability.
The audit was intended to influence a class of persons that includes the creditor.
Auditors have no defenses to negligent misrepresentation claims.

questions.explanation: Under the Restatement "actually foreseen" approach, the middle ground most states follow, an auditor can be liable to a limited group whose reliance is actually foreseen. A complaint is sufficient if it alleges the audit was intended to influence the particular class of persons the plaintiff belongs to, without naming the plaintiff in advance. Reasonable foreseeability to anyone is the broader Rosenblum rule, and grapevine plaintiffs come from Murphy v. BDO Seidman in California, not the Restatement.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-1: "Legal Liabilities of Auditors: An Overview" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 14 (Negligent Misrepresentation (particular classes of persons))
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 18 (Actually Foreseen Third Parties)
Restatement (Second) of Torts §552 (Information Negligently Supplied for the Guidance of Others)
Rusch Factors, Inc. v. Levin, 284 F. Supp. 85 (D.R.I. 1968)
questions.hint: A known class, even without a known name.

questions.prompt:
Investors sue an audit firm for fraud over statements it audited many years earlier. The firm can show the lawsuit was filed long after the legal deadline for this type of claim.

Which defense from your text applies?

options.text: The investors were contributorily negligent because they didn't read the footnotes to the statements carefully.
The auditor's fee was reasonable.
The auditor had no duty to them because it used the firm's standard engagement letter with the client.
The claim is invalid because the statute of limitations has expired.

questions.explanation: Your text lists defenses an auditor can raise against fraud claims: no duty to the third party, the third party's own negligence, work performed under professional standards, no loss, loss caused by other events, and an expired statute of limitations. The filing date makes the limitations defense the fit. The facts say nothing about the investors' care, fees are irrelevant, and an engagement letter doesn't eliminate duties to third parties in fraud cases.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-2: "Auditor Defenses to Negligence and Fraud" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 34 (Auditor Requirements to Protect Themselves Against Fraud)
questions.hint: Look at when the case was filed.

questions.prompt:
Investors claim an auditor committed fraud by signing a clean opinion on statements that hid losses. The auditor shows that every investor in the suit bought shares before the audited statements were released.

Which fraud defense is the auditor using?

options.text: The representation in the audited statements was not material to a reasonable investor.
The auditor followed professional standards.
The third parties did not rely on the representation.
The investors' losses were caused by other events unrelated to the audited statements.

questions.explanation: Reliance is an element of fraud: the third party must have relied on the false representation. Investors who bought before the statements existed couldn't have relied on them. The other choices are also listed defenses, but the facts here (purchase timing) go to reliance, not to materiality, the quality of the audit, or a different cause of loss.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-2: "Auditor Defenses to Negligence and Fraud" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 35 (Requirements For Auditors' Defense Against Fraud)
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 17 (Plaintiff Claims Under Common Law (reliance))
questions.hint: Could they have read the statements before buying?

questions.prompt:
A lender with no contract with the auditor sues in a state that follows Ultramares. The lender alleges the auditor ignored obvious warning signs so completely that it showed reckless disregard for professional standards.

Why can't the auditor win simply by pointing to the lack of privity?

options.text: Ultramares eliminated the privity requirement for all lenders.
Privity is never a valid defense in negligence cases brought by lenders or other creditors.
Ultramares left open gross negligence (constructive fraud) claims, which this is.
The lender is an actually foreseen third party under Credit Alliance.

questions.explanation: Ultramares held that a third party not in privity can't sue for ordinary negligence, but it left open claims for gross negligence and fraud. Gross negligence, or constructive fraud, occurs when the auditor is so careless in applying professional standards that it implies reckless disregard for due care, and it may be interpreted as fraud. Privity is a real defense to ordinary negligence claims, and nothing in the facts sets up a near-privity relationship.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-1: "Legal Liabilities of Auditors: An Overview" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 8 (Liability to Clients: Privity; Ultramares versus Touche)
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 21 (Gross Negligence and Fraud)
Ultramares Corp. v. Touche, 255 N.Y. 170, 174 N.E. 441 (1931)
questions.hint: What did Ultramares leave open?

questions.prompt:
Shareholders sue an auditor under Section 11 of the Securities Act of 1933, pointing to an error in a footnote in the registration statement. The auditor argues the error was so minor that it wouldn't have deterred an average prudent investor from buying the shares.

Which defense is the auditor raising?

options.text: The due diligence defense
The lack of privity defense
The materiality defense
The good-faith defense under Section 18

questions.explanation: Under Section 11, auditors are liable for untrue statements or omissions of material fact in a registration statement. A material fact is one that, if correctly stated, would have deterred or tended to deter the average prudent investor from buying. Arguing the error doesn't meet that test is the materiality defense. Due diligence is about having conducted a reasonable investigation, privity isn't required under Section 11, and the good-faith defense belongs to Section 18 of the 1934 Act.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-3: "Statutory Liability" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slides 38–39 (Securities Act of 1933; Materiality Defense)
Securities Act of 1933 §11, 15 U.S.C. §77k
Your PA Attempt 2 (passed), Q24: same concept, WGU-keyed answer
questions.hint: Would the average prudent investor care?

questions.prompt:
An investor sues an auditor under Section 18 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 over a misleading 10-K. The auditor claims it acted in good faith with no knowledge the statements were misleading. Evidence shows the auditor skipped basic procedures across the whole engagement.

Why might the good-faith defense fail?

options.text: Courts have limited the defense when the auditor's conduct is grossly negligent.
Section 18 provides no defenses of any kind for auditors, only for the company and its officers.
The good-faith defense applies only under Section 11.
Good faith is a defense only for the company's officers, who sign the 10-K, and not for its auditors.

questions.explanation: Section 18 imposes liability for material false or misleading statements in documents filed with the SEC. An auditor can limit liability by showing it acted in good faith with no knowledge the statement was false or misleading. But a number of courts have limited that defense when the auditor's actions are judged to be grossly negligent, as skipping basic procedures across the engagement suggests.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-3: "Statutory Liability" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 45 (Section 18 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934)
Securities Exchange Act of 1934 §18(a), 15 U.S.C. §78r(a)
questions.hint: Good faith vs. gross negligence.

questions.prompt:
Investors sue a homebuilder's audit firm under Rule 10b-5 after the stock lost 80% of its value. The firm shows the loss happened when the entire housing market crashed, and homebuilders with accurate statements fell just as far.

Which defense is the firm using, based on Maxwell v. KPMG?

options.text: The investors relied too heavily on the audited statements instead of doing their own research.
Auditors can't be sued under Rule 10b-5.
The firm's audit opinion was a statement of fact.
The investors' harm was caused by the market, not by the audit.

questions.explanation:
A Rule 10b-5 plaintiff must prove that its damages resulted from the misstatement. Your slide cites Maxwell v. KPMG for the point that Maxwell's harm wasn't caused by KPMG's audit. Showing that a market-wide crash, not the audit, caused the loss defeats that element. Heavy reliance helps the plaintiff, auditors can be sued under 10b-5, and calling the opinion a fact would hurt the firm.

Case note: Maxwell v. KPMG LLP (7th Cir. 2008) was actually a state-law negligence suit by a bankruptcy trustee, where the court borrowed the securities-law idea of loss causation. Your text places it under Rule 10b-5, so answer it that way on the exam.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-3: "Statutory Liability" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 46 (Section 10 and Rule 10b-5: Maxwell versus KPMG LLP)
Maxwell v. KPMG LLP, 520 F.3d 713 (7th Cir. 2008)
Dura Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Broudo, 544 U.S. 336 (2005) (loss causation)
Your PA Attempt 2 (passed), Q26: same concept, WGU-keyed answer
questions.hint: What caused the loss?

questions.prompt:
In its integrated audit, an audit firm detects a material weakness in a public client's internal control over financial reporting but leaves it out of its report. The company later files a registration statement that includes that report.

According to your text, what liability does the auditor face?

options.text: None, because internal control reports aren't covered by securities laws
Liability only to the client, under privity
Section 11 liability under the Securities Act of 1933
Only a PCAOB inspection comment

questions.explanation: SOX requires the auditor to assess management's report on internal controls and issue its own report. Your slides state that failing to disclose detected material weaknesses exposes auditors to Section 11 liability. This is part of how SOX increased auditors' liability by expanding the third parties to whom they owe a duty of care. It isn't limited to the client or to inspection findings.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-5: "SOX and Auditor Legal Liabilities" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 54 (SOX and Auditor Legal Liabilities: Section 404 Internal Control over Financial Reporting)
Sarbanes-Oxley Act §404(b), 15 U.S.C. §7262(b)
PCAOB AS 2201 (An Audit of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting That Is Integrated with An Audit of Financial Statements)
Your PA Attempt 2 (passed), Q27: same concept, WGU-keyed answer
questions.hint: Your slide on SOX §404 names the exposure.

questions.prompt:
In a securities fraud case, the jury finds an audit firm 15% responsible for the investors' losses and finds that the firm knowingly participated in the fraud.

Under the PSLRA, how much of the damages can the firm be required to pay?

options.text: Only 15%, because the PSLRA always limits auditors to their proportionate share
Nothing, because the company that issued the statements is primarily responsible for the fraud
Half, because the PSLRA splits damages equally between defendants
All of the damages, because knowing violators remain jointly and severally liable

questions.explanation:
The PSLRA replaced joint-and-several liability with proportionate liability for non-knowing securities violations, so a defendant pays only its share. Only those who commit knowing securities fraud remain jointly and severally liable. Because the jury found knowing participation, the firm can be made to pay all the damages. The tempting choice is 15%, which would apply only if the violation weren't knowing.

Real rule detail: for non-knowing defendants, the PSLRA can also add up to 50% more of their share if other defendants can't pay (15 U.S.C. §78u-4(f)(4)).
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-4: "Private Securities Litigation Reform Act (PSLRA)" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 52 (Proportionate Liability – PSLRA)
Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995, 15 U.S.C. §78u-4(f) (proportionate liability)
Your PA Attempt 2 (passed), Q29: same concept, WGU-keyed answer
questions.hint: Was the violation knowing?

questions.prompt:
Investors sue an audit firm under the PSLRA. To show the firm acted with scienter, their complaint alleges only that the firm wanted to keep its audit fees and that the client's managers wanted a high stock price.

Why is this allegation likely to fail?

options.text: Generic motives don't show a concrete and personal benefit from the fraud.
The PSLRA does not require any showing of scienter.
Motive can never be used to plead scienter under the PSLRA, no matter how specific the facts are.
Only the SEC, not private investors, can allege scienter against an auditor in a securities case.

questions.explanation: The PSLRA requires particularized allegations creating a strong inference of scienter: strong circumstantial evidence of conscious misbehavior or recklessness, or facts showing both motive and opportunity. Motive must be a concrete and personal benefit from the fraud. Keeping stock prices high, or other motives most insiders and firms share, isn't enough. In Tellabs the Supreme Court added that the inference of scienter must be cogent and at least as compelling as any opposing inference, which is the "reasonable person" idea in WGU's key.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-4: "Private Securities Litigation Reform Act (PSLRA)" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slides 51–52 (Private Securities Litigation Reform Act (PSLRA); Proportionate Liability – PSLRA (Tellabs))
15 U.S.C. §78u-4(b)(2) (required state of mind)
Tellabs, Inc. v. Makor Issues & Rights, Ltd., 551 U.S. 308 (2007)
Your PA Attempt 2 (passed), Q30: same concept, WGU-keyed answer
questions.hint: What kind of motive counts under the PSLRA?

questions.prompt:
A U.S. shipping company's agent pays a small fee to a foreign customs clerk to process the company's paperwork faster. Approving the paperwork is part of the clerk's routine duties, and the company qualifies for it either way.

How does your text classify this payment under the FCPA?

options.text: A bribe, because any payment to a foreign official is illegal under the FCPA
A reasonable and bona fide expenditure
A violation of the books-and-records provision by definition
A facilitating payment, not a bribe

questions.explanation: A bribe is given to get someone to do something that isn't part of their legal or authorized duties. A facilitating payment speeds up a task that is within the person's normal authorized activities, like tipping a maître d' for a better table. The FCPA has an exception for facilitating payments for routine governmental action, though your slides note such payments may still be illegal for the official to receive under local law, and the company must still record them accurately. The bona fide expenditure defense covers things like travel to demonstrate products.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-6: "Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA)" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 58 (Difference between Facilitating Payments and Bribe)
Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, 15 U.S.C. §78dd-1(b) (exception for routine governmental action) and §78dd-1(f)(3)
Your PA Attempt 2 (passed), Q25: same concept, WGU-keyed answer
questions.hint: Was the clerk asked to do something outside his normal duties?

questions.prompt:
The SEC charges a public company under Section 13(b)(2)(A) of the Exchange Act because its books badly misrecorded payments to a foreign sales agent. The company argues no one intended to deceive anyone; the records were just sloppy.

Why does this argument fail?

options.text: The FCPA applies only to private companies, so a public company can't be charged under it.
Careless recordkeeping is a defense only under Section 11 of the Securities Act of 1933, not the Exchange Act.
Scienter is not an element of the books-and-records and internal-controls provisions.
The SEC must first prove a bribe was paid.

questions.explanation:
The FCPA's accounting provisions require SEC registrants to make and keep books and records that accurately and fairly reflect transactions, and to maintain adequate internal accounting controls. Scienter is not an element of these provisions, so lack of intent is no defense to a civil books-and-records charge. The FCPA applies to issuers as well as private companies (the anti-bribery provisions), and a books-and-records violation doesn't require proof of a bribe.

Real rule detail: criminal liability under these provisions does require knowing conduct (15 U.S.C. §78m(b)(5)).
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-6: "Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA)" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slides 48–49 (Liability for Internal Controls Over Financial Reporting 2; SEC Rule 13(b)(2) of the Exchange Act)
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slides 59–60 (Internal Accounting Control Requirements; Section 13(b)(2)(B) Internal Control Requirements)
Securities Exchange Act of 1934 §13(b)(2)(A)–(B), 15 U.S.C. §78m(b)(2)
questions.hint: Does this provision require intent?

questions.prompt:
Dana, a CPA on an audit engagement, finds a set of unusual journal entries in a client's books. To get quick feedback, she screenshots the entries, with the client's name visible, and posts them in a public online accounting forum asking other professionals what they think.

Under the AICPA Code, how is Dana's conduct best classified?

options.text: A violation of the General Standards rule for lack of competence
An act discreditable to the profession
Acceptable, because she is seeking a second opinion to exercise due care
An impairment of independence caused by a self-review threat

questions.explanation:
WGU keys this kind of conduct as an act discreditable. The Acts Discreditable rule covers a broad range of actions that bring discredit to the profession, including the improper disclosure of confidential information gained through the engagement. Posting identifiable client data publicly does exactly that. Seeking advice is fine only through proper channels (firm consultation, or anonymized facts). It isn't a competence (General Standards) problem, and no self-review threat exists because she isn't auditing her own work.

Textbook vs. current law: in the AICPA Code itself, disclosing client information without consent is primarily a breach of the Confidential Client Information Rule (ET 1.700.001). WGU treats it as an act discreditable, so choose that on the exam.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-6: "Rules for the Performance of Professional Services" section
Your Mintz Ch. 4 slides (2025 release): slides 37, 41 (Rules of Professional Practice; Confidentiality)
AICPA Code of Professional Conduct, ET 1.400.001 (Acts Discreditable) and ET 1.700.001 (Confidential Client Information)
Your PA Attempt 2 (passed), Q1: same concept, WGU-keyed answer
questions.hint: Think about the reputation of the whole profession, not one engagement.

questions.prompt:
Marcus, a CPA who works in industry, has not filed his own federal and state income tax returns for the past three years even though he owed tax each year.

Which rule of the AICPA Code does this conduct most directly violate?

options.text: The Integrity and Objectivity rule
The General Standards rule
The Independence rule
The Acts Discreditable rule

questions.explanation: Failing to file a tax return or pay a tax liability that is due is one of the specific acts discreditable listed in the AICPA Code and in your Mintz slides, along with discrimination and harassment, disclosing CPA exam questions, and negligence in preparing financial statements or records. Integrity and objectivity concern professional services for clients or employers; General Standards concern competence and due professional care in engagements; independence applies only to attest work.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-6: "Rules for the Performance of Professional Services" section
Your Mintz Ch. 4 slides (2025 release): slide 37 (Rules of Professional Practice: Acts Discreditable)
AICPA Code, ET 1.400.030 (Failure to File a Tax Return or Pay a Tax Liability)
Your Objective Assessment notes, Ch. 4 (Acts Discreditable: failure of CPA to pay taxes)

questions.prompt:
During fieldwork, the audit senior proposes an adjustment that would reduce revenue. The client's CFO replies, "Remember who signs your engagement letter. Several firms would love this account." The senior refuses to drop the adjustment and takes the matter to the engagement partner and the firm's risk-management group.

Which threat to independence is the senior working to reduce?

options.text: Financial self-interest
Advocacy
Undue influence
Adverse interest

questions.explanation: An undue influence threat exists when client management uses pressure, such as threatening to replace the firm, to coerce the auditor into a judgment. Escalating within the firm instead of yielding is a safeguard against it. Self-interest is about the auditor's own financial stake (for example, a loan from the client). Advocacy is promoting the client's position. Adverse interest arises when the client and the firm are in, or threaten, litigation against each other.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-2: "AICPA Code: Independence Considerations for Members in Public Practice" section
Your Mintz Ch. 4 slides (2025 release): slides 13–14 (Threats to Independence; Safeguards (Exhibits 4.1, 4.2))
AICPA Code, ET 1.210.010 (Conceptual Framework for Independence: undue influence threat)
Your Objective Assessment notes, Ch. 4 (Undue influence: threat to replace firm)
Your PA Attempt 2 (passed), Q2: same concept, WGU-keyed answer

questions.prompt: Which situation creates an undue influence threat to the audit firm's independence?

options.text: The audit partner's spouse is the client's assistant controller and helps prepare the year-end schedules.
The firm has an outstanding loan from the client, a regional bank, on special terms that are not available to the bank's other borrowers.
Client management says it will change firms unless a skeptical senior is taken off the audit team.
The firm promotes the client's newly issued shares to its other clients at an investor event.

questions.explanation: Client attempts to control staffing or to replace the firm are classic undue influence threats. The spouse in a key accounting role is a familiarity threat. A loan from the client on preferential terms is a self-interest threat. Promoting the client's securities is an advocacy threat.

questions.prompt:
After a smooth audit, an attest client sends the engagement manager an expensive designer watch as thanks. The CPA firm has no written policy on client gifts.

What should the manager do, consistent with the AICPA Code on gifts and entertainment?

options.text: Accept the gift, because the firm's policy does not expressly prohibit it.
Ask the client to present the watch to the CPA firm as a whole instead of to the manager personally.
Accept the gift, but only after the audit report has been released.
Evaluate whether a reasonable observer would see the gift as compromising objectivity.

questions.explanation: Under the Code's conceptual framework, the question is whether a reasonable and informed third party would conclude that objectivity or independence is impaired. For an attest client, accepting a gift impairs independence unless its value is clearly insignificant to the recipient; an expensive watch is not. A silent firm policy is not permission, redirecting the gift to the firm doesn't remove the threat, and timing after the report doesn't help because the relationship continues.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-2: "AICPA Code: Independence Considerations for Members in Public Practice" section
AICPA Code, ET 1.285.010 (Offering or Accepting Gifts or Entertainment: gifts from attest clients must be clearly insignificant)
AICPA Code, ET 1.210.010 (Conceptual Framework for Independence: reasonable and informed third party test)
AICPA Code, ET 1.120.010 (Offering or Accepting Gifts or Entertainment: threats acceptable only when reasonable in the circumstances)
Your PA Attempt 2 (passed), Q3: same concept, WGU-keyed answer
questions.hint: The test is how it looks to an informed outsider.

questions.prompt:
An attest client invites the audit manager to an annual customer-appreciation dinner and baseball game that the client also hosts for its key vendors and customers. The manager would attend with client executives.

How does the AICPA Code treat this entertainment?

options.text: It is acceptable if it is reasonable in the circumstances (nature, frequency, value, purpose).
It always impairs independence, because any entertainment received from an attest client is prohibited by the Code.
It is acceptable without any evaluation, because other vendors were invited too.
It is acceptable only if the manager reimburses the client for the full cost.

questions.explanation: The Code treats gifts and entertainment differently. Gifts from an attest client must be clearly insignificant. Entertainment is allowed when it is reasonable in the circumstances, judged by factors such as its nature, the occasion, cost and frequency, whether it has a business purpose, and whether client personnel attend. A blanket ban overstates the rule, an invitation list doesn't remove the need to evaluate, and reimbursement is not required.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-2: "AICPA Code: Independence Considerations for Members in Public Practice" section
AICPA Code, ET 1.285.010 (Offering or Accepting Gifts or Entertainment: entertainment must be reasonable in the circumstances; listed factors)
AICPA Code, ET 1.120.010 (Offering or Accepting Gifts or Entertainment)
questions.hint: Gifts and entertainment have different tests.

questions.prompt:
Hollis & Co. CPAs keeps the books and prepares the tax returns for Ridgeview Bakery, a small private company. A competing firm claims Hollis has violated the AICPA Independence Rule by providing both services.

Has Hollis violated the Independence Rule?

options.text: Yes, because providing two services to one client creates a familiarity threat.
No, because the client is the main beneficiary and keeps management responsibility
No, because the firm assigns different CPAs to the bookkeeping work and to the tax work.
Yes, because combining the services jeopardizes the public interest.

questions.explanation:
WGU keys this as no violation, reasoning that the client is the main beneficiary of the services. Under the AICPA Code, bookkeeping and tax preparation are permitted nonattest services. If Ridgeview is also an attest client, they are allowed when the client assumes all management responsibilities, designates a competent person to oversee the services, evaluates the results, and accepts responsibility for them. Using different staff doesn't create or cure independence, and there is no automatic familiarity or public-interest violation.

Textbook vs. current law: the Code's real test is the general requirements for nonattest services (ET 1.295.040), including that the CPA not assume management responsibilities (ET 1.295.030), not who benefits. For an SEC issuer audit client, SOX bans bookkeeping outright (see the next question).
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-2: "AICPA Code: Independence Considerations for Members in Public Practice" section

AICPA Code, ET 1.295.030 (Management Responsibilities) and ET 1.295.040 (General Requirements for Performing Nonattest Services)

questions.prompt:
Arden Manufacturing, an SEC registrant, asks its external audit firm to take over its bookkeeping and to prepare its federal income tax return.

What is the correct analysis under SOX and the SEC/PCAOB independence rules?

options.text: The firm may do both, as long as different partners lead the bookkeeping engagement and the tax engagement.
No bookkeeping for an issuer audit client; tax work only with audit committee preapproval.
The firm may do both, as long as the fees are disclosed in the proxy statement.
The firm may do neither, because SOX bans all tax services for audit clients.

questions.explanation: Section 201 of SOX lists nonaudit services an auditor may not provide to an issuer audit client, including bookkeeping, financial information systems design, appraisal, actuarial, internal audit outsourcing, management functions, broker-dealer, and legal services. Tax services are not banned, but they must be preapproved by the audit committee (also PCAOB Rule 3524). Staffing and fee disclosure don't cure a prohibited service, and SOX doesn't ban tax services outright.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-2: "AICPA Code: Independence Considerations for Members in Public Practice" section

questions.prompt: Which fee arrangement is prohibited under the AICPA Code's contingent fee rule?

options.text: A fee for preparing a nonattest client's original income tax return, set as a percentage of the refund
A fee for merger advisory work for a nonattest client that is payable only if the acquisition actually closes
A fee contingent on the outcome of an IRS-initiated examination of a client's return
A disclosed commission from a software vendor on a sale to a nonattest client

questions.explanation: Contingent fees are permitted for advisory work for nonattest clients, but are prohibited for preparing an original or amended tax return or claim for refund, for any client. A fee based on the findings of a governmental agency, such as an IRS-initiated examination, is an allowed exception. A disclosed commission from a nonattest client's purchase is permitted under the commissions rule.

questions.prompt:
While preparing this year's return for a corporate client, a CPA discovers that last year's return, which another preparer filed, understated taxable income by a material amount.

What is the CPA's responsibility?

options.text: Tell the client about the error and its consequences, and recommend a correction.
File an amended return for the client as soon as possible.
Report the error to the IRS, since the understatement is material.
Wait to see whether the IRS selects last year's return for examination before doing anything.

questions.explanation: Under Circular 230 and the AICPA Statements on Standards for Tax Services, a CPA who learns of an error or omission must promptly advise the client of it and the possible consequences, and recommend corrective measures. The taxpayer decides whether to correct it. The CPA may not file an amendment without the client or disclose the error to the IRS without consent (confidentiality), and waiting is not acceptable.

questions.prompt:
At the planning meeting, the audit partner tells the team: "Don't take management's word for anything. Keep a questioning mind and critically assess every piece of evidence you collect."

Which principle of the AICPA Code is the partner emphasizing?

options.text: Objectivity and independence
Integrity
The public interest
Due care

questions.explanation:
WGU keys this as due care. Due care requires competence and diligence, and professional skepticism (a questioning mind and critical assessment of audit evidence) is how auditors exercise it. Integrity is honesty and not subordinating judgment; objectivity and independence are freedom from conflicts and bias. The public interest is the broader duty to the people who rely on the work.

Textbook note: your slides tie skepticism to independent thought, objectivity, and due care together, and the KPMG framework says auditors should approach matters "with objectivity and independence." That's why the objectivity choice is tempting. Choose due care when the facts are about questioning and assessing evidence.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-1: "What is Professional Judgment in Accounting?" section

What should they do?

questions.prompt: Why do external auditors communicate audit matters, such as disagreements with management and estimates, to the audit committee rather than to management or the full board?

options.text: Every board member has a financial stake in the company's stock price.
The audit committee is independent of the company's management.
Board members as a group are not familiar with accounting practices.
The audit committee's role is to protect the interests of the auditors.

questions.explanation:
WGU keys this as the audit committee being independent of the company. Under SOX Section 301, audit committee members are independent directors, and the committee is directly responsible for appointing, paying, and overseeing the external auditor, which keeps the audit free of management influence. External auditors communicate accounting policies, estimates, and potential violations of law to it. The other choices are overgeneralizations, or reverse whose interests the committee serves (investors, not auditors).

Textbook note: the audit committee is a committee of the board, so it isn't literally outside the company; its members are independent of management.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 3 (begins p. 102), LO 3-6 (Sarbanes-Oxley and corporate governance)

Sarbanes-Oxley Act §301 (Exchange Act §10A(m))
