questions.prompt:
An audit senior finds evidence that a client is inflating revenue and reports it to her CPA firm's leadership, which decides not to act. She wants to go to the authorities but worries that disclosing client information would break confidentiality rules.

What recourse does Dodd-Frank give her?

options.text: Blow the whistle on her CPA firm for failing to report the wrongdoing
Let the firm's leadership decide, since it has the final say on reporting
Report the client's fraud straight to the SEC, bypassing the firm's own failure
Resign from the firm, since resigning ends her disclosure responsibilities

questions.explanation:
WGU keys this as blowing the whistle on the CPA firm. SEC whistleblower rules let an auditor or an auditor's employee make a submission alleging that the firm failed to assess, investigate, or report wrongdoing as Section 10A requires, or failed to follow other professional standards. Reporting under Dodd-Frank sets aside the confidentiality requirement. Leaving it to leadership ignores her obligation. Resigning doesn't end the auditor's disclosure responsibilities to the SEC. Going straight to the SEC about the client is the tempting choice, but WGU keys the firm-failure route, because her engagement information about the client is generally excluded.

Textbook vs. current law: under SEC Rule 21F-4(b)(4)(iii)(D), information an auditor learns on a required engagement about the client's violation generally isn't "original information" unless a (b)(4)(v) exception applies: preventing substantial injury, the client impeding an investigation, or 120 days after reporting internally. Information about the audit firm's own failure to follow Section 10A or professional standards isn't covered by that exclusion. That's why the key focuses on the firm's failure.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 3 (begins p. 102), LO 3-7: "Whistleblowing" section
Your Mintz Ch. 3 slides (2025 release): slides 63, 65–66 (Dodd-Frank; External Auditor Eligibility; Integrity Considerations)
SEC Rule 21F-4(b)(4)(iii)(D) and (b)(4)(v), 17 C.F.R. §240.21F-4 (auditor exclusion and its exceptions)
Your Objective Assessment notes, Ch. 3 (Dodd-Frank sets aside confidentiality; resignation does not negate disclosure responsibilities)
Your PA Attempt 2 (passed), Q18: same concept, WGU-keyed answer
questions.hint: Whose failure can an auditor report under the whistleblower rules?

questions.prompt:
During an audit, the auditor finds an illegal act that has a material effect on the financial statements. Senior management and the board fail to take timely remedial action.

Under Section 10A of the Securities Exchange Act, what must happen next?

options.text: Report to the board; if the board doesn't notify the SEC within one business day, the auditor does.
The auditor must notify the SEC immediately, before telling management or the board.
The auditor may resign from the engagement quietly, which ends all of its reporting obligations.
The auditor must issue a public statement to shareholders describing the illegal act.

questions.explanation: Section 10A (added by the PSLRA) requires the auditor to report to the board when management doesn't remediate a material illegal act. The board must notify the SEC within one business day and send the auditor a copy. If the auditor doesn't receive the copy, it must give the SEC its own report within one business day, or resign and furnish its report to the SEC within one business day after the board's failure to notify. The process runs through the client's internal channels first, and resigning doesn't end the obligation.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 3 (begins p. 102), LO 3-7: "Whistleblowing" section
Your Mintz Ch. 3 slides (2025 release): slide 67 (Accountants' Obligations for Whistleblowing (Section 10A steps))
Securities Exchange Act §10A(b), 15 U.S.C. §78j-1(b)
Your Objective Assessment notes, Ch. 3 (report to BOD, then SEC if no action)
questions.hint: Internal channels first, and the clock is one business day.

questions.prompt:
Under deadline pressure, an auditor notices several round-dollar entries posted by the CFO after year-end. The auditor knows they are risky but decides not to test them to save time, and signs an unqualified opinion. The entries were material misstatements that caused heavy losses.

Which basic theory of liability best fits the auditor's conduct?

options.text: Opportunity
Recklessness
Intent to deceive
Rationalization

questions.explanation: Recklessness is conduct short of actual intent to cause harm but greater than simple negligence: the auditor knowingly takes a risk, here by deliberately skipping work on entries they knew were suspicious. Negligence would be unknowingly taking a risk; intent to deceive (scienter) means knowing the statements were false. Opportunity and rationalization are fraud-triangle elements, not theories of auditor liability.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-2: "Auditor Defenses to Negligence and Fraud" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 13 (Recklessness)
Your Objective Assessment notes, Ch. 8 (recklessness: knowingly taking a risk)
Your PA Attempt 2 (passed), Q21: same concept, WGU-keyed answer
questions.hint: Did the auditor know of the risk, or know the numbers were false?

questions.prompt:
Shareholders sue an audit firm for fraud after it signed a clean opinion on statements that hid an asset misappropriation scheme.

What must the shareholders specifically prove to hold the firm liable for fraud, rather than negligence?

options.text: That the firm failed to exercise due care
That the firm breached its duty of care to the client
That the firm did not follow GAAS
That the firm acted with intent to deceive (scienter)

questions.explanation: Fraud requires scienter: the intent to deceive, manipulate, or defraud, shown by acting with knowledge that a representation was false or with reckless indifference to its truth. Lack of due care, breach of the duty of care, and GAAS departures support negligence claims but don't, by themselves, prove fraud. Fraud doesn't occur by accident.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-2: "Auditor Defenses to Negligence and Fraud" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slides 17, 21, 33, 62 (Plaintiff Claims Under Common Law; Gross Negligence and Fraud; Auditor Defenses to Fraud; Concluding Thoughts)
Ernst & Ernst v. Hochfelder, 425 U.S. 185 (1976) (scienter required under Rule 10b-5)
Your PA Attempt 2 (passed), Q20: same concept, WGU-keyed answer
questions.hint: What is the key element that separates fraud from negligence?

questions.prompt:
The client sues its auditor for malpractice after employees stole inventory over two years. The auditor shows that the client ignored repeated written warnings about weak warehouse controls.

What is the auditor's most appropriate defense?

options.text: Argue lack of privity, since the client never contracted with the auditor
Use contributory negligence to be completely absolved of any liability
Assert comparative negligence to apportion the damages
Invoke the audit-interference rule to put all of the fault on the client

questions.explanation: Courts now let accountants assert comparative negligence, which replaced the harsh all-or-nothing contributory negligence approach with an allocation of fault, and juries apportion damages between the accountant and the client. The client is in privity with the auditor, so lack of privity fails. Contributory negligence as a complete bar is the outdated approach. The audit-interference rule limits the client-negligence defense to cases where the client actually interfered with the audit; it doesn't let the auditor shift all fault to the client.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-2: "Auditor Defenses to Negligence and Fraud" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slides 11–12 (Defending Audit-Malpractice Cases; Comparative Negligence)
Your Objective Assessment notes, Ch. 8 (comparative negligence: allocation of fault)
Your PA Attempt 2 (passed), Q23: same concept, WGU-keyed answer
questions.hint: Modern courts allocate fault rather than all-or-nothing.

questions.prompt:
Investors sue an auditor under Section 11 of the Securities Act of 1933 over misstatements in audited financial statements included in a registration statement.

What must the auditor show to win with a due diligence defense?

options.text: The plaintiffs did not read or rely on the registration statement when they bought the securities.
The misstatement was not material to an average prudent investor.
The statute of limitations had already expired before the investors filed the suit.
It made a reasonable investigation and had reasonable grounds to believe the statements were true.

questions.explanation: The due diligence defense for an expert such as an auditor under Section 11(b)(3) requires showing a reasonable investigation and reasonable grounds for believing the expertised statements were true. In other words, the auditor wasn't negligent or fraudulent. Lack of reliance, immateriality, and the statute of limitations are separate defenses, not due diligence. Section 11 plaintiffs generally don't have to prove reliance at all.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-3: "Statutory Liability" section

Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slides 38, 40–42 (Securities Act of 1933; Section 11 of the 1933 Act; Section 11 Liability Standard for Auditors; the §11(b)(3) due diligence defense itself isn't on the slides)
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 31 (Auditor Defenses for Negligence: reasonable care and diligence)
Securities Act of 1933 §11(b)(3), 15 U.S.C. §77k(b)(3)
Your PA Attempt 2 (passed), Q24: same concept, WGU-keyed answer

questions.prompt:
A U.S. company's regional director pays a local agent a large "consulting fee" to win approval of a foreign operating license. When charged under the FCPA, the director argues he did not know the agent would pass money to a government official.

Which amendment to the FCPA set the "knowing" standard this defense relies on?

options.text: The Trade Act of 1974
The Federal Trade Commission Act
The International Anti-Bribery and Fair Competition Act of 1998
The Omnibus Trade and Competitiveness Act of 1988

questions.explanation:
WGU keys the Omnibus Trade and Competitiveness Act of 1988. It amended the FCPA to replace the looser "reason to know" standard for payments through third parties with a "knowing" standard, added the affirmative defenses (local law; reasonable and bona fide expenditures), and clarified the facilitating-payment exception. The 1998 act extended the FCPA to foreign companies and persons; the other acts aren't FCPA amendments.

Textbook vs. current law: "knowing" includes awareness of a high probability that the payment would reach an official (willful blindness). A director who deliberately avoids learning the facts can still be liable.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-6: "Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA)" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slides 57–58 (FCPA; Difference between Facilitating Payments and Bribe; the 1988 amendment isn't on the slides)
Omnibus Trade and Competitiveness Act of 1988, Pub. L. 100-418, §5003(a), 102 Stat. 1415
FCPA knowledge definition, 15 U.S.C. §78dd-1(f)(2)
Your PA Attempt 2 (passed), Q25: same concept, WGU-keyed answer
questions.hint: Which 1988 law rewrote the FCPA's knowledge standard and defenses?

questions.prompt:
A U.S. equipment maker pays airfare and modest hotel costs for foreign health-ministry officials to visit its U.S. plant and see a demonstration of the devices the ministry is considering buying.

Which FCPA affirmative defense applies?

options.text: The local law defense
The facilitating payment exception
The bona fide expenditure defense
The materiality defense

questions.explanation: The FCPA allows reasonable and bona fide expenditures, such as travel and lodging, directly related to promoting, demonstrating, or explaining products or services, or to performing a contract. The local law defense requires that the payment be lawful under the foreign country's written laws. The facilitating-payment exception covers small payments to speed up routine governmental actions, not travel to market products. Materiality isn't an FCPA defense.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-6: "Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA)" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slides 57–58 (FCPA; Facilitating Payments vs. Bribes; the affirmative defenses aren't on the slides)
FCPA affirmative defenses, 15 U.S.C. §78dd-1(c)(1)–(2)
Your PA Attempt 2 (passed), Q28: same concept, WGU-keyed answer
questions.hint: Travel tied to demonstrating products: which defense?

questions.prompt:
An investor sues an audit firm under Rule 10b-5, claiming millions in losses after the client's stock collapsed. The firm shows the stock fell along with the whole sector during a market-wide crash.

Which defense does the precedent in Maxwell v. KPMG LLP support?

options.text: The investor's loss was a direct result of the misleading statements in the audit opinion.
The investor's harm was caused by the market in general, not by the auditor's statements.
The firm acted intentionally, so the PSLRA limits its damages.
The firm cannot be sued under Rule 10b-5, because it is not the issuer.

questions.explanation:
A Rule 10b-5 plaintiff must prove, among other elements, that the damages resulted from the misstatement: loss causation. In Maxwell v. KPMG, the court found the harm wasn't caused by KPMG's audit; the company's collapse came from broader market forces. So a firm can defend by showing the loss came from the market, not its statements. The first choice is the plaintiff's argument. Intentional conduct removes protection rather than adding it, and auditors can be sued under 10b-5.

Case note: Maxwell v. KPMG LLP, 520 F.3d 713 (7th Cir. 2008) was actually a state-law negligence suit by marchFIRST's bankruptcy trustee, not a 10b-5 case. Judge Posner borrowed the securities-law idea of loss causation and held that the dot-com bust, not KPMG's audit, caused the collapse. Your text places it under Rule 10b-5, so answer it that way on the exam.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-3: "Statutory Liability" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 46 (Section 10 and Rule 10b-5: Maxwell versus KPMG LLP)
Maxwell v. KPMG LLP, 520 F.3d 713 (7th Cir. 2008)
Dura Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Broudo, 544 U.S. 336 (2005) (loss causation)
Your PA Attempt 2 (passed), Q26: same concept, WGU-keyed answer
questions.hint: What did the court say actually caused the harm?

questions.prompt: According to your Mintz text, which law increased auditors' liability by specifying or expanding the scope of third parties to whom an auditor owes a duty of care?

options.text: The Dodd-Frank Act
The Private Securities Litigation Reform Act
The Securities Exchange Act of 1934
The Sarbanes-Oxley Act

questions.explanation:
Mintz states that SOX increases auditor liability to third parties by specifying or expanding the scope of third parties to whom an auditor owes a duty of care, including through the Section 404 internal control reporting requirements. Dodd-Frank deals with whistleblowers and financial reform, the PSLRA limits auditor liability (proportionate liability, pleading standards), and the 1934 Act regulates trading and ongoing reporting.

Textbook vs. current law: who can sue an auditor for negligence is still set mainly by state common law (Ultramares, Credit Alliance, the Restatement, Rosenblum). SOX adds federal duties and reporting, not a new common-law duty. Answer SOX on the exam.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-5: "SOX and Auditor Legal Liabilities" section

Your Objective Assessment notes, Ch. 8 (SOX 404 expands liability of auditor duty of care)

questions.prompt:
A large corporation and its much smaller audit firm are both sued for securities fraud. The jury finds the audit firm 10% responsible and finds it did not knowingly commit the violation.

How does the PSLRA affect the audit firm?

options.text: It pays damages only in proportion to its share of responsibility.
It cannot settle out of court unless the corporation settles too.
It is liable by default, because intent does not have to be established.
It is held to the same standard as the corporation under joint and several liability.

questions.explanation: The PSLRA dropped joint-and-several liability for non-knowing securities violations and adopted proportionate liability: a defendant pays only the share of damages it is responsible for. Only those who knowingly commit securities fraud remain jointly and severally liable. The PSLRA doesn't tie one defendant's settlement to another's, and it raised rather than removed the need to plead scienter.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-4: "Private Securities Litigation Reform Act (PSLRA)" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 52 (Proportionate Liability: PSLRA)
Securities Exchange Act §21D(f), 15 U.S.C. §78u-4(f) (proportionate liability)
Your Objective Assessment notes, Ch. 8 (proportionate liability for non-knowing securities violations)
Your PA Attempt 2 (passed), Q29: same concept, WGU-keyed answer
questions.hint: Knowing vs. non-knowing violations are treated differently.

questions.prompt:
Investors sue a biotech company and its auditor, alleging they overstated a drug trial's success to lift the share price.

Under the PSLRA, what must the investors do to plead the auditor's fraud liability?

options.text: Show only that the investors suffered economic harm from the misinformation
Show facts that a reasonable person would see as intentional conduct by the auditor
Nothing, because the burden of proof shifts to the auditor under the PSLRA
Show that the investors completed their own due diligence on the drug before buying the shares

questions.explanation:
WGU phrases this as showing that a reasonable person would see the firm's actions as intentional. The PSLRA requires plaintiffs to plead with particularity facts giving rise to a strong inference of scienter, through strong circumstantial evidence of conscious misbehavior or recklessness, or through motive and opportunity. Economic loss alone isn't enough, the burden doesn't shift to the auditor, and the investors' own due diligence isn't an element.

Case note: in Tellabs v. Makor (2007), the Supreme Court held a complaint survives "only if a reasonable person would deem the inference of scienter cogent and at least as compelling as any opposing inference one could draw from the facts alleged." That's the source of WGU's 'reasonable person' wording.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-4: "Private Securities Litigation Reform Act (PSLRA)" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slides 51–52 (PSLRA Particularity Standard; Tellabs versus Makor)
Securities Exchange Act §21D(b)(2), 15 U.S.C. §78u-4(b)(2)
Tellabs, Inc. v. Makor Issues & Rights, Ltd., 551 U.S. 308 (2007)

questions.hint: The PSLRA raised the bar for pleading intent.

questions.prompt:
Dana Ruiz, CFO of Halvorsen Freight (a public company), knows the third-quarter 10-Q overstates revenue by $4.2 million through fictitious shipments. She signs the written statement accompanying the report, swearing it fully complies with the Exchange Act and fairly presents the company's financial condition. She does it deliberately to protect the stock price before her options vest.

Which Sarbanes-Oxley section's criminal penalties apply most directly to her willful false statement?

options.text: Section 906
Section 806
Section 103
Section 301

questions.explanation: Section 906 requires the CEO and CFO to furnish a written statement that each periodic report complies with the Exchange Act and fairly presents the company's financial condition, and it attaches criminal penalties: up to $1 million and 10 years for knowingly certifying a noncompliant report, and up to $5 million and 20 years for doing it willfully. Section 806 protects whistleblowers from retaliation, Section 103 directs the PCAOB to set auditing, quality-control and independence standards, and Section 301 covers audit committee independence. On PA Q10 you chose Section 103; the word "willfully" plus a CEO/CFO statement points to 906.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 3 (begins p. 102), LO 3-6
Your Mintz Ch. 3 slides (2025 release): slide 45 ("Section 906")
Notes, Ch. 3 (SOX 906)
Sarbanes-Oxley Act §906, 18 U.S.C. §1350(c)
questions.hint: Which section adds criminal penalties to the CEO/CFO written statement?

questions.prompt:
The SEC finds that the CEO of Marlowe Biotech signed certifications stating he had evaluated the company's disclosure controls and had disclosed all significant internal-control deficiencies to the auditors and audit committee. In fact, he never reviewed the controls and knew of two deficiencies he didn't disclose. Federal prosecutors are separately weighing criminal charges.

Which statement correctly matches the Sarbanes-Oxley sections to this conduct?

options.text: Section 302 is the criminal certification provision, and Section 906 governs the auditor's attestation on internal controls.
Section 404 requires the CEO's certification, and Section 806 sets the criminal penalties for false certifications.
Section 906 applies only to the CFO's statement, and Section 302 applies only to the CEO's statement.
Section 302 covers the false certification about controls (civil SEC action); Section 906 adds criminal penalties.

questions.explanation: Section 302 requires the CEO and CFO to certify each periodic report, including that they evaluated disclosure controls and disclosed significant deficiencies to the auditors and audit committee, and false certifications support SEC enforcement (Mintz's QSGI example). Section 906 is the separate criminal certification that the report complies and fairly presents. Section 404 covers management's internal-control report and the auditor's attestation, and 806 is whistleblower anti-retaliation. Both 302 and 906 apply to both the CEO and the CFO. This builds on your PA Q10 miss by pairing 302 with 906.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 3 (begins p. 102), LO 3-6
Your Mintz Ch. 3 slides (2025 release): slides 44–46 (SOX 302, 906; QSGI case)
Notes, Ch. 3 (SOX 302, 906)
Sarbanes-Oxley Act §302 (15 U.S.C. §7241) and §906 (18 U.S.C. §1350)
questions.hint: One section is the civil certification about controls; the other carries prison time.

questions.prompt:
The founders of Verdant Outfitters tell the board: "If we adopt conscious capitalism, we should stop worrying about profit entirely and put every dollar into social and environmental programs." A board member objects that this misreads the approach.

Which statement reflects conscious capitalism as Mintz describes it?

options.text: Profit still matters, but decisions serve a higher purpose and create value for all stakeholders.
The founders are right, because conscious capitalism replaces the profit motive with social and environmental goals.
Conscious capitalism means maximizing shareholder profit while staying within the rules of the game.
Conscious capitalism requires giving every employee stock options so they share in the profits.

questions.explanation: Mintz's first guiding principle says that while "profits are essential for a sustainable business, conscious capitalism focuses on purpose beyond profit," and decisions follow a stakeholder model that weighs effects on the whole ecosystem. Eliminating profit, the founders' view, was your answer on PA Q12, and it's the trap. Maximizing profit within the rules is Friedman's economic model (managerial capitalism). Stock options for everyone isn't part of the approach.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 3 (begins p. 102), LO 3-5
Your Mintz Ch. 3 slides (2025 release): slides 38–40 (Conscious Capitalism; Economic Model of CSR)
Notes, Ch. 3 (Conscious Capitalism: purpose beyond profit)
Mackey & Sisodia, Conscious Capitalism (2013): four tenets
questions.hint: Purpose beyond profit isn't the same as no profit.

questions.prompt:
Tidewater Grocers has adopted conscious capitalism. In her first all-hands meeting, the new CEO commits to "embrace our purpose, create value for every stakeholder, and inspire the actions that build a conscious culture," and she starts doing so herself.

Which of the four guiding principles of conscious capitalism is the CEO personally modeling?

options.text: Higher purpose
Stakeholder orientation
Conscious culture
Conscious leadership

questions.explanation: Mintz defines conscious leadership as leaders who "embrace the company's purpose, create value for all stakeholders, and inspire actions that contribute to a conscious culture." Higher purpose is the company's reason for existing beyond profit. Stakeholder orientation is optimizing value for all stakeholders as a decision model. Conscious culture is the resulting climate of trust, care and cooperation. All four are real principles; the clue is that one person, the leader, is acting. This reinforces the conscious capitalism concept you missed on PA Q12.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 3 (begins p. 102), LO 3-5
Your Mintz Ch. 3 slides (2025 release): slide 38 (Conscious Capitalism: 4 Guiding Principles)
Notes, Ch. 3 (Conscious Capitalism)
questions.hint: The quote describes what a person at the top does.

questions.prompt:
At Ridgeline Software, sales vice presidents pressure the accounting staff to book fourth-quarter deals early because the VPs' bonuses depend on quarterly revenue. The CEO wants to stop the pressure without scrapping a compensation plan that otherwise works well.

Which action best addresses the problem, according to Mintz?

options.text: Have top management set the tone, backing staff who refuse and making integrity outrank the target.
Eliminate all incentive pay across the company so that no one has any reason to manipulate the results.
Move the accounting department so that it reports to the audit committee instead of management.
Remove supervisors from the whistleblowing process so that all reports go straight to human resources.

questions.explanation: Mintz stresses that "support for ethical behavior from top management is a critical component of fostering an ethical climate," and that poor tone at the top discourages reporting and invites manipulation. Scrapping incentive pay was your answer on PA Q13. It treats a symptom, and the pressure can return in other forms if leadership doesn't model integrity. The audit committee oversees financial reporting but doesn't manage the accounting department. Rerouting all reports to HR doesn't change the culture driving the pressure.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 3 (begins p. 102), LO 3-3: "Ethics in the Workplace" section
Your Mintz Ch. 3 slides (2025 release): slides 13, 24 (poor tone at the top; Ethics in the Workplace)
Notes, Ch. 3 (fraud reporting discouraged by poor tone at top)
COSO, Internal Control—Integrated Framework (2013), Principle 1: commitment to integrity and ethical values
questions.hint: Fix the culture, not just the pay plan.

questions.prompt:
At Pellham Industries, the CEO tells managers, "Make the numbers, whatever it takes." Over the past year, two accountants who questioned aggressive estimates were transferred to remote offices, and other staff have stopped raising concerns.

Which two of Marianne Jennings' seven signs of ethical collapse do these facts show?

options.text: A weak board of directors, and conflicts of interest that are overlooked
Innovation like no other company, and goodness in some areas that atones for evil in others
Young 'uns with a bigger-than-life CEO, and a weak board of directors
Pressure to maintain numbers, and fear and silence

questions.explanation: Jennings' signs include "pressure to maintain numbers" ("financial results at all costs") and "fear and silence," where employees stay quiet because people who raise issues are "ignored, treated badly, transferred, or worse." The facts say nothing about the board's independence, conflicts of interest, claims of unique innovation, or philanthropy used to excuse misconduct. Nothing indicates a CEO surrounded by inexperienced loyalists either.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 3 (begins p. 102), LO 3-2: "Seven Signs of Ethical Collapse" section
Your Mintz Ch. 3 slides (2025 release): slides 19–21 (Seven Signs of Ethical Collapse; Fear of Reprisals)
Jennings, The Seven Signs of Ethical Collapse (2006)
questions.hint: Look at the CEO's words and what happened to the people who spoke up.

questions.prompt:
After a lunch meeting where five nurses at Cedar Valley Hospital discussed chronic understaffing, one of them posts a summary on LinkedIn "on behalf of our unit," calling the staffing levels unsafe. No coworkers comment on the post. The nurses aren't unionized. The hospital fires her for disloyalty.

Is her post likely protected under the National Labor Relations Act?

options.text: No, because only one employee posted and none of her coworkers commented online.
Yes, but only if the nurses belong to a union that has approved the post.
Yes, because posting on behalf of coworkers about shared conditions is concerted activity.
No, because she had to raise the concern internally before posting publicly.

questions.explanation: NLRA Section 7 protects employees' right to engage in "concerted activities for the purpose of … mutual aid or protection," with or without a union. Activity is concerted when it's taken with or on the authority of other employees, such as a post summarizing a group discussion and made on the unit's behalf, about shared working conditions. A single poster with no comments was your answer on PA Q14. The deciding fact is the group backing, not the number of online replies. Mintz's slide uses coworker comments as its example of concerted activity, but comments are only one way to show group action; a post made on the group's behalf after a group discussion also qualifies. No union membership or internal-reporting step is required.

questions.prompt:
An employee posts on Facebook that she's angry about being passed over for a raise. As it stands, the NLRB would likely treat the post as an unprotected "personal gripe."

Which added fact would most likely make the post protected concerted activity?

The employee posted after work hours from her own personal phone rather than a work device.
Coworkers join the thread about how the raise policy affects them all and plan to act together.
The employee had already filed a formal complaint about the raise with human resources.

Coworkers discussing a shared pay policy and planning group action is the classic trigger. Union membership, timing, device, and prior HR complaints don't turn an individual gripe into group activity. This is the contrast behind your PA Q14 miss.

questions.prompt:
The CEO of Brightwater Bank notices that branch managers routinely cut ethical corners to hit loan-volume targets. She wants to replace this "whatever it takes" mindset with a lasting ethical climate.

Which change would do the most to achieve her goal?

options.text: Have the external auditor take over from internal audit in checking compliance with the ethics policy.
Tell managers to use their own professional judgment to decide what is ethical in each situation they face.
Build ethical conduct into performance evaluations and reward behavior that reflects the bank's values.
Raise the loan targets so that only the most capable managers advance.

questions.explanation: Mintz's list of measures for an ethical culture includes "reward ethical behavior and include in performance evaluation system," so people see that values, not just volume, drive advancement. Using external auditors to police the ethics policy was your answer on PA Q16. The external audit is an opinion on the financial statements; Mintz assigns ethics-policy checks to internal auditors. The CFO, since ethics compliance is mainly a financial reporting matter.
Each department head, reviewing the conduct of his or her own team.
The internal auditors, who act as the audit committee's "eyes and ears."

It would require auditors to resign from the firm before they could report anything.

The program doesn't change PCAOB inspections, doesn't require resignation, and doesn't remove the firm's Section 10A duties. On PA Q18 you chose reporting the client directly. No. Resigning doesn't negate an auditor's disclosure responsibilities to the SEC.
Yes. Only current employees of an audit firm may make SEC whistleblower submissions.
No, but she must first obtain the client's written consent before contacting the SEC.

Whistleblowing in conformity with Dodd-Frank "sets aside [the] confidentiality requirement," and the AICPA confidentiality rule permits disclosures required by law, so she needs no client consent. Based on Erhart v. BofI Holding, what is the likely outcome?

He is protected only if he has already received a Dodd-Frank whistleblower award.
He is protected only if he first gave the documents to a newspaper so the public could see them.
The suit will likely fail, because confidentiality agreements don't override federal whistleblower rights.

BofI Holdings: it "clarifies that employer confidentiality agreements do not supersede federal whistleblower rights," "signals that retaliatory lawsuits against whistleblowers are unlikely to succeed," and gives guidance on using company documents. (The court weighed whether the documents taken were reasonably related to the claims.) Protection doesn't depend on getting an award, and going to the press isn't the protected channel. This connects to your PA Q18 worry about breaking confidentiality.

questions.prompt:
An external auditor concludes that a public client committed an illegal act with a material effect on the financial statements. Senior management hasn't taken remedial action, so the auditor reports directly to the board. The board must notify the SEC within one business day, but the auditor receives no copy of any notice.

Under Section 10A of the Securities Exchange Act, what must the auditor do?

options.text: Give the SEC its own report within one business day, or resign and still send it in that window.
Wait until the next annual audit, then raise the matter with the full board of directors again.
Issue a press release describing the illegal act so that current and future investors are warned.
Mail a letter to the company's shareholders explaining the problem.

questions.explanation: Section 10A(b), added by the PSLRA, sets the sequence: report to management and the audit committee, report to the board if there is no timely remedial action, and the board notifies the SEC within one business day and sends the auditor a copy. If the auditor doesn't receive the copy, it must furnish its report to the SEC within one business day, or resign and still furnish the report no later than one business day after the board's failure to notify the SEC. Mintz adds that the matter must go through the client's internal system before the auditor turns to the SEC. Press releases and shareholder letters aren't part of the statutory process.

After a $3 million embezzlement, the new CEO of Hollis Manufacturing tells the board that the most important internal-control fix isn't another approval form. It's the integrity and ethical values that management shows, its commitment to competence, and the board's oversight.

Monitoring
Risk assessment
Control environment

It's the foundation set by tone at the top, the integrity and ethical values management demonstrates, and board oversight. Control activities are specific policies and procedures, like approvals and reconciliations. Monitoring evaluates whether controls keep working, and risk assessment identifies risks to objectives. Mintz adds that even good controls give only reasonable assurance and can be overridden by top management, which is why tone matters (the lesson of PA Q13).

A signed annual code-of-conduct acknowledgment
The external audit of the financial statements
Management certification of the financial statements

questions.prompt:
A director of Larkspur Homes votes to have the company buy a parcel of land from an LLC she secretly owns, at 30% above appraised value. She doesn't disclose her interest to the board.

Which fiduciary duty has she most clearly breached?

options.text: The duty of loyalty, because she put her personal interest ahead of the corporation's
The duty of care, because she failed to act as an ordinarily prudent person would
No fiduciary duty, because directors owe their duties only to the CEO
The confidentiality duty in the AICPA Code of Professional Conduct

questions.explanation: Directors and officers are fiduciaries. The duty of loyalty requires acting "in the best interest of [the] corporation," and an undisclosed self-dealing transaction at an inflated price is the textbook loyalty breach. The duty of care concerns diligence and prudent decision-making in good faith; it's a weaker fit when the core problem is a conflict of interest. Directors owe duties to the corporation and its shareholders, not to the CEO, and the AICPA Code governs CPAs' professional conduct, not directors' fiduciary duties.

questions.prompt:
An engineer at Coastline Devices finds that a cardiac monitor the company sells can fail without warning. She reports it to her supervisor and then, with no action taken, to the board, keeping detailed test records throughout. The board does nothing. She believes going public will force a recall.

Under Richard DeGeorge's criteria, is it morally permissible for her to blow the whistle publicly?

options.text: No, because loyalty to the employer always outweighs any duty to report harm to people outside the company.
Yes, but only if she will receive a financial award from a regulator for reporting the defect.
Yes, because the harm is serious, she went up to the board, and she has evidence and expects change.
No, because whistleblowing is permissible only when the harm is to the company itself.

questions.explanation: DeGeorge holds that corporations have "a moral obligation not to harm." His conditions for permissible whistleblowing are serious and considerable harm to others, reporting to the supervisor and taking the matter "all the way up to the board," documented evidence that would convince "a reasonable and impartial observer," and a reasonable belief that going public will create change worth the personal risk. All are met here. Loyalty doesn't override preventing serious harm, an award isn't a moral criterion, and the concern is harm to others such as patients, not to the company.

1% to 5% of the monetary sanctions collected
30% to 50% of the monetary sanctions collected
A flat $1 million, regardless of the sanctions

Lena, a CPA who works as controller at Ardent Pharma, is unsure how to account for unreleased clinical-trial costs. She posts her employer's confidential cost data, with the product name visible, on a public accounting forum to ask other professionals for their opinion.

The General Standards Rule, because she lacks competence in pharmaceutical accounting
The Acts Discreditable Rule, by disclosing confidential information obtained through her employment
The Accounting Principles Rule, because the cost data hasn't been reported under GAAP

Posting it publicly is the violation, whatever her reason. Members in business aren't subject to the Independence Rule; preparing an attest client's statements, your answer on PA Q1, is an independence issue for firms. A CPA firm's ethics committee is reviewing four complaints.

Which complaint describes a violation of the Acts Discreditable Rule?

options.text: An audit senior prepares adjusting journal entries for an attest client and makes the final decisions on them.
An audit partner repeatedly sexually harasses a staff accountant on the engagement team.
A partner accepts an audit in an industry he has never served and makes no plan to build competence.

Making management decisions for an attest client, the kind of choice you made on PA Q1, impairs independence. Taking an engagement without the needed competence violates the General Standards Rule. questions.prompt:
Kara, a CPA, prepares only the tax returns for a restaurant owner; her firm does no attest work for him. The owner invites Kara and her husband to a $400 dinner and concert, where he plans to discuss next year's tax planning. Her firm has no policy on client entertainment.

What should Kara do under the AICPA Code?

Accept if the entertainment is reasonable in the circumstances.
Decline, because the Code prohibits accepting any entertainment from any client.
Accept, but only after the tax engagement has ended.

questions.explanation: For non-attest clients, the Code's gifts-and-entertainment interpretation under the Integrity and Objectivity Rule asks whether accepting is "reasonable in the circumstances." Kara weighs the nature, value, frequency and timing of the entertainment, whether it has a business purpose, and whether a reasonable observer would doubt her objectivity. Having the client address it to the firm, your answer on PA Q3, doesn't change the threat. There's no blanket ban, and a missing firm policy doesn't end the analysis. Waiting until the engagement ends isn't the test.

Accept, because the gift's value is clearly insignificant to each recipient.
Accept, but only if the client gives the umbrellas to the firm instead of to individuals.
Accept, but disclose the gifts in a note to the audit report.

Entertainment is judged by whether it's reasonable in the circumstances. A $35 logo umbrella is clearly insignificant. Contrast this with an expensive watch, which would impair independence. Redirecting a gift to the firm doesn't change the analysis (your answer on PA Q3), and audit reports don't disclose gifts.

For three years, Cole & Pratt CPAs has processed payroll and prepared tax returns for Lindell Bakery, with no audits, reviews, or other attest work. Now the bakery's bank wants audited financial statements, and the bakery asks Cole & Pratt to perform the audit.

What changes for the firm?

options.text: Yes. If a service is immaterial to consolidated results, independence is automatically preserved.
Yes. The audit committee can waive any independence requirement it considers immaterial.
No. It rests on SEC and PCAOB rules, judged by a reasonable investor who knows all the facts.
No. Independence matters only in appearance to outside investors, not in fact.

questions.explanation: Mintz frames the materiality debate with a pointed question: is independence "left to the individual judgment of the auditors or is it based on SEC regulations and PCAOB standards?" The SEC's general standard asks whether a reasonable investor with knowledge of all relevant facts would conclude the auditor isn't capable of objective and impartial judgment. Materiality doesn't automatically preserve independence (the reasoning behind PA Q6). An audit committee pre-approves permitted services but can't waive prohibitions. The SEC requires independence both in fact and in appearance.

questions.prompt:
While preparing Luis Ortega's 2025 tax return, his new CPA discovers that his 2024 return, prepared by another firm, left out $18,000 of freelance income reported on a Form 1099.

What must the CPA do under Circular 230 and the AICPA tax standards?

options.text: Report the omission to the IRS, since the CPA now knows the 2024 return is wrong.
File an amended 2024 return on Ortega's behalf to fix the omission.
Do nothing, because another firm prepared the 2024 return and is responsible for it.
Promptly tell Ortega about the omission and its consequences; whether to amend is his call.

questions.explanation: Circular 230 §10.21 requires a practitioner who knows a client didn't comply with the tax law, or made an error or omission on a return, to promptly advise the client of it and its consequences. The AICPA SSTS similarly require informing the taxpayer and recommending corrective measures, and the taxpayer decides whether to amend. The CPA doesn't notify the IRS, which would breach confidentiality; that was your answer on PA Q7. The duty applies even though another preparer did the earlier return, and the CPA can't amend it without the client's decision.

questions.prompt:
A CPA is representing her client in an IRS examination of his 2024 return. During the exam, she discovers an error on that return that increases his tax. She tells the client, but he refuses to let her disclose it to the IRS agent.

What is the CPA's most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Tell the IRS agent about the error herself, since the exam is already under way.
Correct the 2024 return herself and hand the corrected version to the agent.
Continue the representation and make statements to the agent that hide the error.
Keep it confidential, consider withdrawing, and recommend that the client get legal advice.

questions.explanation: SSTS guidance on representation says the member must act with integrity and follow the Confidential Client Information Rule. When a taxpayer won't correct an error, the member considers whether to continue the relationship and recommends legal consultation. Circular 230 (§10.51(a)(4)) also bars knowingly giving false or misleading information to the IRS, so she can't help conceal the error. Without the client's consent, she can't disclose it herself; that would repeat the PA Q7 trap of reporting to the IRS. Only the taxpayer can correct the return.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-7: "Ethics and Tax Services" section

questions.prompt:
Last year, Hearthstone Retail's allowance for doubtful accounts was $1.2 million. This year a recession has doubled customer delinquencies. The auditor starts with last year's $1.2 million and nudges it up to $1.3 million, without building an estimate from current aging data.

Which judgment trap does this show?

options.text: Anchoring tendency
Availability tendency
Confirmation tendency
Overconfidence tendency

questions.explanation: Anchoring is starting from an initial value and adjusting too little. Here, last year's balance anchors the estimate despite a major change in conditions. Availability means relying on whatever information comes to mind most easily. Confirmation means seeking evidence that supports an initial belief, and overconfidence means overestimating one's own ability or knowledge. KPMG's framework counters all four by calling for "critical assessment of audit evidence" and System 2 thinking.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-1: "What is Professional Judgment in Accounting?" section

questions.prompt:
An audit senior evaluated a goodwill impairment question carefully. She defined the issue, considered alternative approaches, gathered and weighed evidence, and reached a well-supported conclusion. But she never wrote down why she reached it, and a reviewer can't follow her reasoning.

Which step of the KPMG Professional Judgment Framework did she skip?

options.text: Clarify issues and objectives
Consider alternatives
Articulate and document the rationale
Gather and evaluate information

questions.explanation: The KPMG framework's steps are: clarify issues and objectives, consider alternatives, gather and evaluate information, reach a conclusion, and articulate and document the rationale. She completed the first four. Without documentation, a reviewer can't evaluate the judgment, and the auditor can't later show she exercised due care. The other steps were all done.

questions.prompt:
A CPA licensed in State X learns that the state board of accountancy's rule on a client-records issue is stricter than the AICPA's rule on the same point.

Which rule should she follow?

options.text: The state board of accountancy's rule
The AICPA rule, because it's the national standard
Whichever rule is less restrictive
Whichever rule the client prefers

questions.explanation: Mintz notes that "when differences exist between AICPA and those of the licensing state board of accountancy, the CPA should follow the state board's rules." The state board issues and can revoke her license, so its rules control. A CPA can't choose the less restrictive rule, and client preference doesn't change professional obligations.

A senior on the audit of Brookfield Plastics takes out a $40,000 personal loan from an individual who owns 15% of Brookfield's outstanding stock, on terms not available to the general public.

Undue influence threat
Financial self-interest threat
Management participation threat

The auditor now has a personal financial stake in the relationship. Familiarity comes from close or long relationships, such as a spouse who's the CEO. Undue influence is pressure such as a threat to replace the auditor. Management participation means taking on management functions.

Advocacy threat
Adverse interest threat
Familiarity threat

questions.explanation: Exhibit 4.1's example of an advocacy threat is "promoting the client's securities as part of an initial public offering or representing a client in U.S. tax court." The firm is championing the client's position rather than evaluating it objectively, and the SEC's principles say an auditor can't serve in an advocacy role. Self-review means auditing one's own work, adverse interest arises when the firm and client are opponents, and familiarity comes from close relationships.

questions.prompt:
Ellis, an audit partner, retires from his CPA firm and becomes CFO of Wren Industries, a privately held audit client. The firm wants to keep auditing Wren.

Which conditions must be met for the firm's independence not to be impaired?

options.text: Wren must give the firm written consent, and Ellis must agree not to discuss the audit.
Ellis may keep consulting for the firm part-time, as long as he's paid hourly.
The firm must disclose Ellis's new role at Wren in a paragraph of its audit report each year.
Any amounts owed him are immaterial, and he can't influence or appear associated with the firm.

questions.explanation: Mintz lists the conditions for a former partner or professional employee who joins an attest client in a key position. Amounts due to him must not be material to the firm, he must not be able to influence the firm's operations or financial policies, and he must not participate in or appear to be associated with the firm. Continuing to consult for it or being named in firm literature counts as participating. Client consent and audit-report disclosure aren't the tests. (For public-company clients, SOX also imposes a one-year cooling-off period for certain roles.)
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-2: "AICPA Code: Independence Considerations for Members in Public Practice" section

questions.prompt:

options.text: Both services are permitted, as long as the fees are disclosed in the proxy statement.
Actuarial services are prohibited; tax services are allowed with audit committee pre-approval.
Both services are prohibited for a public company audit client.
The actuarial services are allowed, but tax services are prohibited.

questions.explanation: SOX Section 201 lists prohibited nonaudit services for issuer audit clients, including bookkeeping, financial information systems design, appraisal or valuation, actuarial services, internal audit outsourcing, management functions, broker-dealer and investment services, and legal and expert services unrelated to the audit. Tax services aren't prohibited, but they "must be preapproved by the audit committee." Disclosing fees doesn't make a prohibited service permissible.

questions.prompt:
A client wants to deduct an aggressive expense. After research, his CPA concludes the position has a reasonable basis but doesn't meet the realistic possibility standard. The client notes that his chance of being audited is under 1%.

Under the AICPA Statements on Standards for Tax Services, what may the CPA do?

options.text: Recommend the position without disclosure, since the chance of audit is so low.
Recommend the position without disclosure, as long as the client signs a waiver.
Recommend it only if she advises the client to disclose it to the taxing authority.
Never recommend it, because every position must meet the realistic possibility standard.

questions.explanation: The SSTS let a member recommend a position or sign a return that has at least a realistic possibility of being sustained. A position that only has a reasonable basis is allowed if the member advises the taxpayer to disclose it appropriately. The SSTS also forbid positions that exploit a taxing authority's audit selection process, so the low audit odds are no reason to skip disclosure. A client waiver can't substitute for disclosure. The answer that bans all such positions ignores the disclosure exception.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-7: "Ethics and Tax Services" section

questions.prompt:
A CPA is asked to represent two business partners before the IRS in a dispute in which their interests directly conflict. She believes she can represent each of them competently and diligently, and the representation isn't prohibited by law.

Under Circular 230, what else is required for her to proceed?

options.text: Oral consent from whichever partner pays the larger share of the fee for the representation
Each client's informed consent, confirmed in writing within 30 days
Written approval from the IRS examining agent
Nothing more, because a conflict of interest can never be waived

questions.explanation: Circular 230 §10.29 allows representation despite a conflict if the practitioner reasonably believes she can competently and diligently represent each client, the representation isn't prohibited by law, and each affected client gives informed consent, confirmed in writing within a reasonable period and no later than 30 days. Mintz notes a contrast: the AICPA Code doesn't let a CPA waive a conflict in a representation that requires independence. Consent from only one client isn't enough, and the IRS doesn't approve waivers.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-7: "Ethics and Tax Services" section
Your Mintz Ch. 4 slides (2025 release): slides 51–52 (Circular 230: Conflicts of Interest; Waiver)

questions.prompt:
Prospect CPAs runs this ad: "Our team includes three former IRS agents, so we can get your audit dropped."

Does the ad comply with the AICPA Advertising and Other Forms of Solicitation Rule?

options.text: Yes, because the AICPA now permits all forms of advertising.
No, but only because it doesn't state the firm's fees.
No, because it implies an ability to influence a government body.
Yes, as long as the team really does include former IRS agents.

questions.explanation: Advertising and solicitation are permitted, but not in a false, misleading or deceptive manner. Mintz lists implying "ability to influence official bodies" as prohibited, along with coercive or harassing solicitation and misleading fee representations. A literally true statement about the staff doesn't save a claim that suggests improper influence, and the rule has no requirement to state fees.

questions.prompt:
A state board-authorized peer review team reviewing Hale & Company CPAs asks for the working papers from a client audit. The client hasn't consented to sharing its information.

May the firm provide the working papers?

options.text: Yes, because an authorized peer review is an exception to the confidentiality rule.
No, not without first getting the client's specific written consent to the disclosure.
Only if the peer reviewers first obtain a validly issued subpoena for the papers.
No, because working papers can never leave the firm.

questions.explanation: The Confidential Client Information Rule bars disclosure without the client's consent, but Mintz lists exceptions: responding to a validly issued subpoena or summons, complying with laws and regulations (such as Dodd-Frank whistleblowing), a peer review authorized under the PCAOB, AICPA, state CPA society, or board of accountancy, and defending the CPA in an investigation. The peer review exception means no client consent or subpoena is needed.

questions.prompt:
An auditor failed to detect a payroll fraud at Kestrel Foods, and Kestrel sues for audit malpractice. The jury finds the auditor 60% at fault, and finds Kestrel 40% at fault for ignoring the auditor's written recommendation to separate payroll duties. Damages total $500,000.

In a jurisdiction that allows a comparative negligence defense, how much does the auditor owe?

options.text: $0, because any negligence by the client completely bars recovery
$500,000, because the auditor was in privity with the client
$300,000, its 60% share of the damages
$200,000, the client's 40% share of the damages

questions.explanation: Comparative negligence "replaced the harsh all-or-nothing approach of contributory negligence with a formula based upon allocation of fault." Courts let accountants assert it and have upheld juries' apportionment of damages between the accountant and the client. Here that's 60% of $500,000, or $300,000. A $0 result is the old contributory-negligence outcome. Privity creates the auditor's duty to the client but doesn't eliminate apportionment, and $200,000 is the client's share, not the auditor's. This is the defense you missed on PA Q23.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-2: "Auditor Defenses to Negligence and Fraud" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slides 11–12 (Defending Audit-Malpractice Cases; Comparative Negligence)
Notes, Ch. 8 (comparative negligence: allocation of fault)
Restatement (Third) of Torts: Apportionment of Liability §7 (2000)
questions.hint: Fault is split, so damages are split.

questions.prompt:
An auditor defending a malpractice suit argues that the client's own negligence should reduce or bar its recovery. The court applies the audit-interference rule.

Under that rule, when can the client's negligence serve as a defense?

options.text: Whenever the client was negligent in any part of its business, even if the negligence was unrelated to the audit
Only when it contributed to the auditor's failure to perform the audit and report the truth
Always, because the rule shifts all fault for the loss onto the client
Only when the engagement letter disclosed the client's negligence in advance

questions.explanation: Mintz explains that the client's negligence "is a defense only when it has contributed to the accountant's failure to perform his contract and to report the truth." That's the audit-interference rule, and it narrows the defense; it doesn't widen it. Courts don't let auditors escape by pointing to unrelated client carelessness. The rule never shifts all fault to the client, the misreading behind your PA Q23 answer. The correct choice there was comparative negligence. Engagement letters don't control this test.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-2: "Auditor Defenses to Negligence and Fraud" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 11 (Defending Audit-Malpractice Cases)
Notes, Ch. 8 (contributory negligence of the client)
Lincoln Grain, Inc. v. Coopers & Lybrand, 345 N.W.2d 300 (Neb. 1984)
questions.hint: The client's negligence has to affect the audit itself.

questions.prompt:
Investors sue the auditor of Ridgeway Homes under Rule 10b-5 after Ridgeway's stock collapses. The auditor shows that every homebuilder's stock fell 70% to 80% in the same period because of a nationwide housing crash, regardless of how each company was audited.

Which element of the investors' claim is the auditor attacking, based on Maxwell v. KPMG?

options.text: Loss causation: the misstatement, not other events, must have caused the loss.
Scienter: the plaintiffs must show that the auditor intended to deceive.
Materiality: the plaintiffs must show that the misstatement mattered to investors.
Privity: the plaintiffs must show a contract with the auditor.

questions.explanation: Mintz summarizes Maxwell v. KPMG, a malpractice suit by the bankruptcy trustee of marchFIRST: "Maxwell's harm wasn't caused by KPMG's audit"; the dot-com collapse was. The same loss-causation principle applies to Rule 10b-5 claims (Dura Pharmaceuticals v. Broudo). The defenses Mintz lists include "any loss to the third party was caused by other events." Scienter and materiality are separate elements, and the facts here go to causation. Rule 10b-5 doesn't require privity. On PA Q26 you chose the plaintiff's argument; the defense is that market-wide events caused the loss.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-3: "Statutory Liability" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slides 34, 46 (Auditor Requirements to Protect Themselves; Section 10 and Rule 10b-5)
Maxwell v. KPMG LLP, 520 F.3d 713 (7th Cir. 2008)
Dura Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Broudo, 544 U.S. 336 (2005)
questions.hint: Would the stock have fallen anyway?

questions.prompt:
A law student asks which Sarbanes-Oxley requirement most directly expanded auditors' exposure to claims by third parties.

Which answer reflects Mintz's explanation?

options.text: Section 806, which protects employees who report fraud from retaliation
Section 906, which imposes criminal penalties on CEOs and CFOs for false certifications
Section 404, which requires the auditor to report on internal control over financial reporting
Section 301, which requires public companies to have an independent audit committee

questions.explanation: Mintz states that SOX "increases auditor liability to third parties by specifying or expanding the scope of third parties to whom an auditor owes a duty of care." It requires accounting firms to assess management's internal-control report and issue their own report, and "failing to disclose detected material weaknesses exposes auditors to Section 11 liability." Sections 806, 906, and 301 govern whistleblowers, executives, and audit committees, not the auditor's own reporting duties. On PA Q27 you chose Dodd-Frank; SOX is the law that expanded the auditor's duty.

questions.prompt:
A plaintiff's attorney tells a jury: "The Private Securities Litigation Reform Act and Dodd-Frank expanded the third parties that auditors owe a duty of care to."

What is wrong with the statement?

options.text: The PSLRA generally narrowed auditor liability; SOX is what expanded the duty of care.
Nothing; both laws expanded auditors' duty to all foreseeable investors.
Only the Dodd-Frank part is wrong; the PSLRA did expand auditors' duty of care.
Only state common law, never federal statutes, can change who is owed a duty.

questions.explanation: Mintz describes the PSLRA as an attempt to rein in auditor liability "because tort liability was out of control." It adopted proportionate liability for non-knowing violations and required particularized pleading of scienter. Dodd-Frank's relevant provisions concern whistleblowers. SOX is the law that "increases auditor liability to third parties by specifying or expanding the scope of third parties to whom an auditor owes a duty of care." Federal securities law does shape auditor liability. This targets your PA Q27 miss.

Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995, Pub. L. 104-67

questions.prompt:
In a securities class action, a jury finds that an audit firm didn't knowingly commit the violation and assigns it 15% of the responsibility for $20 million in damages. The issuer, which is 85% responsible, is bankrupt, so its share can't be collected. The plaintiffs are large institutional investors.

Under the PSLRA, what is the audit firm's maximum exposure?

options.text: $4.5 million: its $3 million share plus up to 50% more toward the uncollectible amount
The full $20 million, because the defendants are jointly and severally liable
$0, because the bankrupt issuer bears primary responsibility for all of the damages
$3 million, its proportionate share, with no possibility of paying any more

questions.explanation: The PSLRA "drops legal standards of joint-and-several liability and adopts proportionate liability" for defendants who didn't knowingly violate the law, so the firm starts with its 15% share, $3 million. When another defendant's share is uncollectible, proportionately liable defendants can be made to cover part of it, capped at 50% of their own share; here that's $1.5 million more. Only defendants who knowingly commit fraud face full joint and several liability, which was your answer on PA Q29. The other choices ignore either the firm's share or the reallocation rule.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-4: "Private Securities Litigation Reform Act (PSLRA)" section

Notes, Ch. 8 (proportionate liability for non-knowing violations)
Securities Exchange Act §21D(f), 15 U.S.C. §78u-4(f)(2), (f)(4)
questions.hint: Proportionate share, plus a capped reallocation.

questions.prompt:
In the same case, one plaintiff is a retired teacher whose recoverable damages are $40,000. Her net worth is $150,000.

How does the PSLRA treat her claim against the proportionately liable audit firm for the bankrupt issuer's uncollectible share?

options.text: The firm owes her only its 15% share, with no exceptions for individual investors.
The firm is jointly and severally liable to her for the uncollectible share, as a small investor.
She can't recover from the auditor at all, because only institutional investors may sue.
She must prove the firm acted knowingly before she can recover anything.

questions.explanation: The PSLRA's proportionate liability has a small-investor exception. If a defendant's share is uncollectible, proportionately liable defendants are jointly and severally liable for that share to an individual plaintiff whose recoverable damages exceed 10% of her net worth, when that net worth is under $200,000. She qualifies, since $40,000 is about 27% of $150,000. Individuals can sue, and she doesn't need to prove knowing fraud for this exception. This extends the PSLRA rule you missed on PA Q29.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-4: "Private Securities Litigation Reform Act (PSLRA)" section

questions.prompt:
An auditor plainly failed to follow GAAS when testing inventory. But the client sold the business at a price that wasn't affected by the inventory figures, and it can't identify any money it lost because of the faulty audit. It sues for professional negligence anyway.

Which element of a negligence claim is the client missing?

options.text: Duty
Damage
Breach of duty
Privity

questions.explanation: Professional negligence requires four elements. Duty: the accountant owed the plaintiff reasonable care. Breach: the accountant failed to use the skill normally possessed by public accountants. Damage: the plaintiff suffered damage. Causation: a causal nexus connects the breach and the damage. The auditor owed the client a duty and breached it by ignoring GAAS, but with no loss, there's no damage, so the claim fails. Privity isn't an element of negligence itself; it decides which third parties can sue.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-1: "Legal Liabilities of Auditors: An Overview" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 10 (Professional Negligence)
Notes, Ch. 8 (professional negligence must have duty, breach, damage, causation)
